subtopic: NUMBER OF CASES REPORTED-STEPS TO REDUCE INCIDENCE

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: NUMBER OF CASES REPORTED-STEPS TO REDUCE INCIDENCE
speechtext:
I
should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, of which I gave him notice. In view of the fact that this is the season in which Canadian fathers and mothers generally stand in considerable fear of the dread malady, infantile paralysis, I was wondering whether the minister could give the house some information as to the number of cases recorded at the present time. What, step is the department taking in conjunction and collaboration with the provincial governments to try to reduce the incidence of this disease if possible?

speakeroldname: Hon. PAUL MARTIN (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: NUMBER OF CASES REPORTED-STEPS TO REDUCE INCIDENCE
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman did give me notice yesterday of his question. We have established communication with each province, and periodically, three times a week as a matter of fact, we receive a report from them by telegram as to the actual number of cases in the various provinces. Of course my hon. friend will realize that constitutionally the matter of
Inquiries of the Ministry

communicable diseases is under the jurisdiction of the provinces. The last summary is as follows:	British Columbia, 42, and thirtyfour of these cases are from Vancouver; Saskatchewan, 5; Alberta, 6 up to July 5; Manitoba, 2; Ontario, 19; Quebec, 21. Montreal has had two local and five outside cases only since January of 1947; New Brunswick, 3; Nova Scotia, 4 and Prince Edward Island, 1.
It is early in the epidemic season for forecasting, and one can only say that few areas as yet are showing abnormally high rates. One of these is Vancouver. The incidence of paralysis as yet in the Vancouver cases is reported as being minimal.
Our role is to aid the provinces. It is thought, both by the provinces and by ourselves, at the moment that the most effective way of extending it is by the extension of information. To that end we have arranged for the distribution of a pamphlet called "Polio Facts", which contains valuable information for lay people about the disease. We are also giving attention to the mobilization, in conjunction with the provinces, of polio emergency volunteers for use in highly epidemic areas. These lay volunteers have been found useful by the national foundation for infantile paralysis in the United States, and in Canada in the Montreal health department. The basic information about this has been forwarded to British Columbia and to the other provinces within the last few months. We have accelerated what we feel to be our special field, that of research, and to this end we have strengthened the virus section of our laboratory of hygiene here in Ottawa.

apologized for the fact that there was faulty construction because, after all, the thing was dione as a special concession. I do not think that this apology compares very well with the election promises and platforms which the government presented to the veterans in 1945. When one compares the offer held out to the veterans, of a small holding for a maximum of $6,000, of which $1,400 would be written off, so that a satisfactory house on an acre or more of land would be provided, the apology does not jibe very well with the promises ana the inducements. And even the apology itself was delivered in a belligerent tone as though we had no right to criticize the department for these failures or for any shortcomings.
Another hon. member remarked last night that we were making a great cry about nothing, trying to stir up discontent. If the members of the committee think discontent \vould otherwise not exist, I suggest that they visit some of these projects around British Columbia, such as Braefoot, Lulu Island, Kelowna and Vernon. I do not think that question requires answering, because it does not refer to any part of my remarks.
Yes, it does.

The other comment I wish to make, in respect of one matter, is that Sl.200,000 has been authorized so far for repairs to these houses.
In a return I received on June 30 information is contained that Bennett and White, who built all the projects in British Columbia, obtained fees over and above their costs to the extent of $104,000. That amount of money has been paid to Bennett and White for this construction in British Columbia. British Columbia is now having to pay its portion of the extra $1,200,000 for repairs after this work has been completed. The position is, then, that Bennett and White got $104,000 for work on which the Canadian people are having to pay an additional $1,200,000, because it was not satisfactory.
As I have pointed out, the lists of complaints signed with the department show in each house from nine to nineteen major defects. I have given one instance where two support posts were left out of the basement to make room for furnace pipes. They had to be put in subsequently and caused further damage to other rooms in the house consequent upon raising the floor level. That is atrocious construction work. The taxpayer is being asked to bear the cost of putting it right. That is one of the matters which was referred to, and one of the things which leads us to call for a royal commission-I should say not "call" for it, but to dtemand it. Last night when dealing with this matter the parliamentary assistant-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: May I ask a question? Is the hon. member not prepared to leave it to the Department of Justice to decide whether Bennett and White are liable for damages?

That, of course, is not a proper question. The parliamentary assistant said last night that the Department of Justice had been consulted earlier. So far as I know they have not been consulted as a result of the evidence given before the public accounts committee.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
What I am asking for is a royal commission to investigate the matter. It could table its report and then the Department of Justice could give consideration to it. The parliamentary assistant said last night that the matter of requiring the contractors to bear the cost of these repairs is being considered.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask a question, with all respect?
No, not now.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is the hon. member questioning the integrity of Bennett and White? If so, we will have an additional inquiry.
I wish the minister would not interrupt me further.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is typical of your mentality.

The hon. member for Van-couver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) asked whether or not the contractor would be required to pay the costs of the repair work. The official answer from the department on this matter, in a return tabled on July 12 is as follows:
As mentioned, in some instances responsibility for the cost of repairs is to be the subject of discussion and arrangement with contractors.
I suggest that indicates no proper effort to guard the taxpayers' money and to hold these contractors responsible for the damage which I have just set out. As I said, the list indicates faults running from nine to nineteen per house. These are major structural defects, one of which, as I said, was the leaving out of two posts, and other defects of equal importance. I shall not go through the list. But I could mention that in nearly every case the sump pits have been defective and have had to be re-cemented. Cement on the walks around the houses has had to be replaced, and there have been inadequate foundations.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Sheer politics.
The whole matter requires a great deal more positive action on the part of the department than is indicated at the present time.

I shall be only a moment or two. My complaint is on entirely different grounds from those taken by the previous speaker. Without doubt some mistakes have been made in connection with the construction of some of these houses. We have had a parliamentary committee investigating these mistakes for months. That committee has made a report to the house, and I support its con-83166-371J
elusions and recommendations and trust action will result to give effect to those recommendations. The parliamentary assistant has mentioned that there will be adjustments made in the cost of certain houses and that repairs are to be made in the case of others. I do not think the time of the house should be taken up discussing details as to whether the sewer pipe is short or faults of that kind. Let us keep these things in the proper proportions.
The hon. member for Eglinton very forcefully placed the views of his party before the committee last night, and I think that should be sufficient. Only recently I was speaking to a friend who is building a house somewhat similar to the ones being built by V.LA. That house was built under careful supervision. He visited it every day to see what the builder was doing, and checked cost, but it has cost him about thirty per cent more than he expected to pay when he began last year. Recently I read in a Montreal paper a report about a hotel being built there. The president of the company stated that regardless of the most careful computation of costs made only eighteen months ago the hotel will cost thirty per cent more than was anticipated. Private builders are finding the same difficulty. So I say: Let us keep our criticism in proportion. Let us make it having in mind the work of the Department of Veterans Affairs as a whole. Let us not forget the large number of men who have been benefiting by this scheme.
The director is human and no doubt he and his officials have made mistakes. But if the director had not taken any action there would be hundreds of veterans still living in hovels and the like. This scheme has been of great benefit to the veterans of this country, and I believe that if the veterans were consulted the great majority of them would say that the scheme has been worthwhile. I think they appreciate the efforts of the department to do something for them under the difficult building circumstances existing in Canada today.
I come now to my own complaint. There are between 125 and 150 veterans in my riding who are anxious to come under this scheme. Under the changed regulations it is now necessary that a minimum of two acres be obtained, whereas formerly a small holding could consist of not more than half an acre. I ask the minister and the officials to give consideration to these complaints. My constituency is mountainous and land is scarce. For that reason I think special consideration should be given to these men, and they should be permitted to build houses in the vicinity of
Supply-Veterans Affairs

Trail and Nelson on sites smaller than the two acres now required. Two acres are not required in my constituency because you can grow as much on half an acre there as can be grown on two acres in most other parts of Canada. I do hope the minister and his officials will give my veteran constituents consideration in this respect.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The very constructive suggestion of the hon. member certainly will be given consideration.

I wish to associate myself with the hon. member for Selkirk and the hon. member for Yorkton in appealing to the minister and the government again to consider the granting of clear titles to those veterans who were settled under the Soldier Settlement Act of 1919 and who are still indebted to the government. Some of these men are now older citizens and I understand that there are only 3,400 in this category. We owe a debt to these war heroes of 1914-18. I am informed that the actual cancellation of this debt would not involve a large sum of money as far as the government is concerned.
These men were put on the land after the first world war when prices were high. In some cases they were settled on land known as sub-marginall land in the west. It was a most expensive undertaking for them to get started in the purchase of machinery and other equipment. The minister is also aware that when these contracts were originally signed they provided for interest charges of seven per cent on arrears. I know that today under the Veterans Land Act a rate of three and one half per cent is charged and I am glad that is being done. I know also that adjustments have been made in the case of old settlers who settled under the settlement act of 1919, but in making these adjustments there is one which has been overlooked. The most important adjustment of all would be the granting of clear titles.
Those whom I know have worked as hard as their neighbours but they have been the victims of circumstances in the way of poor crops, illness and that sort of thing. For that reason they deserve better treatment. Most of them are men of advanced years and they would like clear titles to the places they call home. They have laboured for over a quarter of a century. This parliament has cancelled war debts and on occasions we have made gifts and granted loans bearing interest of only two per cent. I am not quarrelling with that; I would be the first to support such action, but the fact is that these veterans

are not yet rehabilitated in the strictest sense of 'the word. AVe are spending millions :to help in the rehabilitation of Europe and yet we have not yet completely rehabilitated these men who in most instances are the victims of circumstances. I urge the government to give more consideration to the cancellation of these debts and the issuing of clear titles to these veterans. I believe the hon. member for Yorkton asked how many veterans had paid up their indebtedness in 1946-47 and I do not believe he got a complete answer.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I say with regard to the first part of the hon. member's representations that they will certainly receive very careful attention. With regard to the second question, I doubt if we have figures available for the last year. We gave them for the last five years.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
We gave the figures for
the first six months; are they not satisfactory to the hon. member?

What about the last
six months of last year?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
I can get those and send
them to the hon. member. We had (them for the five years and I thought that would give a better 'picture.
I would like to know what they are for the past year. Can that information be given by provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We will get that right away.
The minister said that he is going to give favourable consideration to these boys, but that is what they have heard for the past thirty years.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I never used the word "consideration", because I hate the word.

The minister said he was going to take it under advisement or something. These boys deserve a little better treatment than that, because they have been asking for this for years. The officials of the department realize that the deal given to these men was quite different from that which has been given to the men of this war, and yet they still fail to take that necessary step. Only yesterday the officials of the department told us that there were about fifteen per cent of these men whom they figured would never be able to make the grade.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
That is hardly correct.
They said that they felt that eighty-five per cent would have no difficulty in meeting their

Supply-Veterans Affairs
obligations, which meant that fifteen per cent might have some difficulty. They did not say that fifteen per cent would not be able to make it.

They are going to have some difficulty in making it. These men are now sixty to sixty-five years of age. How many of that fifteen per cent suffered disabilities as the result of action in the last war?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend knows the details of 'the land settlement far better than I do. Does he not think that it would be better to deal generously with individual cases where a veteran is in danger of being dispossessed from his land, extend every possible consideration to those cases, but that those men who are able to make payments properly to the crown should make them as a matter of equity and justice? I think a blanket policy of cancellation would be unjustified.
I agree with that. I have seen men who have done their best for years and years, and lose the whole thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is my point.

It is a little bit too
late. The fact that the department forecloses and puts men off the land is an injustice.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend can
rely upon the sympathetic consideration of the department in a case such as he has just mentioned so long as I am there anyway.

Consideration came
much too late for most of them.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not think so.

It seems
to me that the estimates of this very important department which were brought before the house yesterday should have been brought in much earlier in the session. Many of us felt that it was going to require some time to iron out some of the difficulties. By leaving the estimates to the last days of the session is not giving us the opportunity to deal with the matter in the way in which we should like to deal with it, nor is it giving the veterans who are depending upon the action of this parliament a fair chance.
In my riding I have a hundred Veterans Land Act houses in the county of Middlesex, townships of Westminster and London. I have taken the opportunity to visit many of them. I am going to be frank and fair. I would say that they are very nice little homes but they
are far too high in price. There are a few defects. The defects are not as great as you will find in many of the farm homes of this country; yet these farmers are expected to carry on under these conditions. I met many of the young veterans who have purchased these places. They are a fine type of young Canadian. I am proud of them. I am going to suggest to the minister and to the government. that the whole thing be reconsidered and that $500 or $1,000, or whatever it is, be written off the cost to give these boys a good chance. They have lost five years of their lives which were spent in the defence of the country. It is going to take them ten years in these years of peace to accomplish as much as they would have accomplished in the five years they lost while the rest of us were getting established in the country. These boys were fighting for us. I doubt whether there is anything that we can do that the country will criticize so long as we give these boys a fair and square deal.
In the particular houses in which I am interested the contract was let to an outside firm, a firm at New Liekeard, Ontario. In the city of London, county of Middlesex, we have as fine contractors as there are anywhere in the country. I am not going to mention any of them, but. I believe a firm in the city of London could have built these houses more quickly and done the job better, and there would not have been the criticism that you had to bring in some outside unknown contractor to build these houses. The work was done wrong end first. The land was fairly heavy clay and needed drainage. They excavated for the basements and the basements remained full of water for weeks and weeks. They then pumped them out and built the foundation. Is' it any wonder that these foundations are cracking, that there are defects? I am not going to go into that. I have a list of defects in several houses, but I shall not go into that now. Some of them have been repaired. Hon. members have mentioned some of these defects.
If the places had been drained at the beginning instead of at the end after the houses were erected, they would have had a good dry foundation and the work would probably have been done better. I am going to say a word about drainage. I have a return which shows that it cost. $16,000 and some odd to do the work. I am not saying that it was excessive, but it sounds like a lot of money back home to the farmers who have done some drainage work of their own. I inspected the drains and the outlets, and they were working satisfactorily. But what is happening is this. Alt
Supply-Veterans Affairs

that- water that used to take probably a week to run off now comes down on the farmers' lands in a very short period of time, and they are hoping that the drainage act will be so used that the Veterans Land Act home owners will be required to pay their just share for the rest of the drainage in that area.
I understand that the parliamentary assistant mentioned the fact that this Veterans Land Act home plan was done in a hurry to accommodate these young men who were returning. I do not think it was done in any great hurry. The operation was started prior to the 1945 election. They have built a hundred houses in the area and they are not completed yet. If that is building in a hurry I do not know what it means.
I am going to refer for a moment or two to farms for veterans. I have one particular case in mind; I have done considerable work on it. This young veteran was born on a farm in Manitoba and has had life-long experience. He knows what he wants and how to do it. After he returned he took a job as a hired man on a farm so that he could get some experience in Ontario ways and so that he would have the opportunity to look around the province of Ontario and get a farm that was suitable. I think he was very wise in that-not to jump at the first place that was offered to him. After some months he decided on a farm in Huron county. I took the opportunity on occasions to discuss this particular farm with the present chairman of this committee, who knows farms. The proper deposit was made and routine inspections wrere made, but the officials and the committee decided that too much money was being asked for it. This took considerable time. The price that was agreed on between the veteran and the owner of the land was some $4,300. The farm consisted, of fifty acres of land. The department turned it down. Opportunity was taken to discuss this matter with the officials in London, and they suggested that it would be handled from the Guelph office. This young veteran went to Guelph and saw the officials there. They suggested that they had other farms that were available and would be more satisfactory. He went out to see one of these farms which consisted of 100 acres. I do not believe it is going to cost $4,300, but a railway crosses it one way and a gully crosses it another.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Will the hon. member give us the name of the gentleman either now or later?

Yes, I will give the name. A lot of the land was not workable. This 100 acre farm was offered him 
as an alternative to the 50 acre farm. He went to the farm this spring. It will be realized that it rained nearly' every day this spring in Ontario. There was a foot and a half of water in the basement of the farm home. You could see the clouds roll by through the kitchen roof. The barn roof leaked. In other words, it was not worth anywhere near $4,300 which the other farm that I mentioned was worth. I understand that a veteran had given this farm up after a trial, yet they tried to saddle this young lad with this poor farm. I venture to say that it will cost in the neighbourhood of $3,000 to put that farm in a habitable condition, on top of the price at which it is-being sold. I said to the young lad, "You ask them to give you a better farm in Huron county, more acres for less money, and you will quickly take it." But they had nothing like that to offer. The price was too high. Get a, better farm for less money and this young man will quickly take it. They have not done that. Some of these young lads have become discouraged because there is so much red tape. I do not know how you are going to get away from it.
As a result of inquiries I have made, I have found that for every ten veteran farmers there is one official of the department in the London district. If this is applied socialism I can see how under a socialist government there would be no unemployment. It is the best advertisement there could be against socialism in the county of Middlesex.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Under the C.C.F. it would be much worse.

I agree
with that.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The parliamentary
assistant is admitting it is bad, then.

I think
that is all I need say about the Veterans Land Act in regard to small holdings. I would not care to repeat what one veteran said about it. He said he could have bought a farm in Lambton county. He had been waiting all summer to make a deal and the whole thing was washed up.
Under the Veterans Land Act, where there are homes scattered through the townships, I think there should be some arrangement between the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Post Office department so that there might be a rural mail delivery. Rural routes coulld easily be extended because there are enough homes to justify it, and it would be a service to some areas. I do not suggest that it would apply to all areas, but in the north

Supply-Veterans Affairs
area of London the mail route should go down the centre of the holdings to deliver mail to these people.	'
Now I want to say a word about Westminster hospital, which is located in my area. I understand that this is the largest military hospital in the British empire, and I am proud that it is in my riding. I am well acquainted with many of the doctors and the officials and have seen the work they are doing not only with mental patients but with those who have lost a leg or an arm or have suffered other disabilities. They are doing fine work. I am also acquainted with many of the staff and I can say that they are very loyal. I have no word of criticism except this, and I find that it applies in all departments. There are some who are employed temporarily and some are permanent. I know one or two men who have worked since the last war and are still temporarily employed. That does not tend to build up loyalty, because such men do not know where they stand. I have taken this matter up with the civil service commission, and my opinion of the relationship that exists between the civil service commission and the various departments of government is that the commission should be jacked up and overhauled. In fact, a whole new commission should be put in, because there is too much red tape now.
Westminster hospital is situated on a highway, a paved road, and a great many people who are on that road are walking back and forth between the hospital and their homes. There is a bus service, I admit, but ninety per cent of the people who walk up and down that highway are going 'to or coming from the hospital and sooner or later someone is bound to be killed on that highway. Recommendations have been made to have a sidewalk extended, but as it goes out past township property and the hospital authorities have intimated from time to time that they would not participate in any expenditure of that kind -and perhaps it would be setting a precedent -I suggest that the municipality and the hospital get together and provide a sidewalk. To some extent the sidewalk would go past farm property, and no farmer wants to pay on a frontage basis.
Before I conclude I would like to bring to the attention of the minister the circumstances of a soldier who was and is now residing in Canada but who served in the British forces in Africa in the first world war. He was disabled there and he is now living in my riding. He is totally disabled. I have taken this matter up with the Canadian and British pension authorities and this is simply
one of those cases where each passes the buck. Lately this man's wife had had to get employment to maintain the home, and I was informed only last week that the job in which she was employed under the unemployment insurance commission has terminated. All he gets is $13 a month. According to some of the regulations there is an alternative pension but he does not seem able to secure it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: How old is he?
Sixty-six.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
He should be able to
apply for the war veterans allowance without difficulty.
I wrote a letter to the British pension authorities and to the Canadian pension commission, but, as I say, each passes the buck. I will give this man's name. His name is Ronald McBain.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext:
Was	he domiciled in
Canada when he went into the British army?
He was here in 1913-1914.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Have you the regimental number?

I have
it in my files.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: Will you send it to me?

Yes. I know that sometimes there is chiselling on the pension commission, but I have seen this man personally and I can assure the minister that he is worn out. He will never be able to work and how he will exist I do not know. I may say that the British pension commission were indignant with me that I should have approached them in the way I did. Apparently the British authorities are more interested in getting money from the taxpayer than they are in taking care of their injured veterans. I am wondering if that is true of all socialist governments. I have taken it up with the Canadian pension authorities and the British and, as I say, each tries to shift it onto the other, and so I am now leaving it with the minister. I realize that he is fair and I know he will give it his personal consideration. I hope these things will be taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I say a word with regard to the three points raised by the hon. member for Middlesex East. In the first place he mentioned certain projects in London. I can assure him that the write-off committee have not yet visited the London area for that
Supply-Veterans Affairs

purpose. But I can assure him that the interests of the veterans in the London area will be amply protected, according to equity and justice.
The second point he mentioned had to do with the Westminster hospital and the question of temporaries and permanents. The reason why it is only on a basis of approximately fifty-fifty is that we are using, in cooperation with the Canadian universities and the Canadian Medical Association, the finest specialists in Canada to give the exservicemen the very best services they can get, as temporary consultants charging specialists' fees for specialist operations or visits. That is the reason for that at the present time.
The third point raised by the hon. member was in regard to the civil service. I can assure him that the question is now under active review by the civil service commission.

I understand that the health centre which was constructed there recently is now to be used as a hospital for tubercular veterans. I hope they will have every success. It is an ideal location. I just wanted to mention that because it was brought to my attention when I was home that this was to take place.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes; because of crowding in other adjacent areas we were compelled to use that for tuberculosis cases. That may be a temporary expedient, but for the time being it is necessary.

There are a couple of non-controversial matters that I wish to bring to the attention of the minister. In my opinion the stand taken by the Veterans Land Act administration in arbitrarily denying to certain areas settlement under the Veterans Land Act is something which must be brought to the attention of the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member to repeat that? I was interfered with.

I am referring particularly to certain areas in Saskatchewan which have been denied settlement under the Veterans Land Act. I refer to one area in particular, namely, the rural municipality of Dufferin; two areas immediately north and south of Bethune, and also the areas in the central part of the province west of Long Lake, in which there has been settlement for many years and in which there are large numbers of successful farmers. The Veterans Land Act administration has refused various veterans the opportunity to take up lands in that area. I wish to place before the committee a resolution which summarizes the

matter for all these areas. It was passed by the rural municipality of Dufferin, No. 190, on November 7, 1946, and a copy forwarded to the Minister of Agriculture. It reads:
We, the ratepayers of the rural municipality of Dufferin No. 190, go on record as condemning the action of the department administering the Veterans Land Act, in not giving assistance to veterans in establishing themselves on land in this municipality, especially to sons of resident farmers who could be assisted from the home farm.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Which area is that?

That is the area immediately west of Long Lake. Farmers have been in that area for many years. Their sons come back from overseas and desire to settle near home. While on occasions there has been a. drought, as in other areas within the Palliser triangle, a ruling once made by the Veterans Land Act administration has been adhered to and these young men who desire to settle adjacent to their own homes have been denied that opportunity.
The second matter has to do with machinery for veterans. On occasions I have brought to the attention of the minister the cases of veterans endeavouring to purchase a tractor, in which they could get no further assistance than a certificate of identification. Certificates of identification do not give any assistance to veterans. The veterans go to the various implement companies or to their local agent and they find that they have no priority. In fact, the department itself admits that it grants no priorities to veterans establishing themselves in agriculture. To use the words of the Veterans Land Act administration, all it does is give the veteran the "breaks", whatever that may mean. I suggest even at this late date that something be done to grant those veterans a priority. I can name four instances of the situation I have described. I do not intend to go into particular cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How recently was that?
Within the last six weeks. I brought one case to the attention of my right hon. friend last December. Last week he was able to advise me that this man could now secure a tractor.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I interrupt, just in order to help?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My information from my officials-and it can be checked up, of course-is that all the machinery companies now give priorities with regard to machinery not only to veterans coming under the Veterans Land Act but also to other veterans

that is, if they have the machinery available.

Supply-Veterans Affairs
When was that ruling made? It must have been within the last three weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.
Then it certainly is not always applied to the veteran.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I should like to help my hon. friend to kick up some trouble about that if it has not been followed out, because that- has been the policy for over a year now.

Yes, I appreciate that it has been the policy. It has been an objective, but in several instances it has not been attained.
I now bring a third problem to the attention of the minister. It has to do with veterans who do not get land under the Veterans Land Act, but who reestablish themselves on their own land. Veterans who get land under the Veterans Land Act receive a discount of seven per cent on purchases. Other veterans are denied1 that discount because of the fact that they are not going to borrow money from the government. I think the discount should apply to all. Certainly we should not penalize the veteran who does not need to borrow $4,000 to $5,000 from the people of this country, who ask for no advance. He should be entitled to the same consideration as the others.
I come now to the next matter arising out of the treatment of those who take land under the Veterans Land Act, and that is in the matter of awaiting-returns benefits. Sufficient attention is not paid to the granting of these awaiting-returns benefits among young men who turn to agriculture. Within the last few days I have received three letters in that connection, and I feel a very close check-up should be made, because from time to time technical excuses are offered for the delays when individual cases are brought to the attention of the administration.
I am going to preface what I desire to say further by stating that I have found this, and I think it has been the experience of members in all parts of this house; that when matters dealing with veterans have to do with pensions or allowances every sympathetic consideration is given by the officials. I think it only fair to make that statement; I say that, however, subject to this: that the sympathetic consideration which characterizes officials of the pension board and war veterans allowance board seems in so many cases to be denied as far as the administration of the Veterans Land Act is concerned.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: If I may interrupt for a second in regard to the awaiting-returns benefits mentioned by my hon. friend, there are more paid in northern Saskatchewan than in any other part of the dominion.

I am not thinking
about the amounts or the numbers. I am thinking about the fact that men have been waiting since they applied as far back as last February and March.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Delays.
Yes. I do not ask for action forthwith after application is made, but I do find that in this branch there is too much delay.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader

I am going to say that I do not think the minister is able to control this, because in this administration there seems to be set up a control distinct and apart from the Department of Veterans Affairs as a whole. The veterans at Normandy Park in Prince Albert, Saskatchewan, were promised their houses at certain definite prices. They took possession of those houses and later were advised that a mistake had been made, or that the houses cost more than the department thought they would, and that they must either pay the additional amount or get out. They received an ultimatum from the director of the Veterans Land Act; they received letters that ought not to be written by government departments or by officials however powerful they may be for the time being. As far as Prince Albert is concerned I took up the matter and pressed for consideration, but I did not get any action. Finally the provincial command of the Canadian Legion took it up, and they were able to have action taken by the director, with the greatest of hesitation, however,'-to use the friendliest word I can think of.

All the way through the piece the attitude of the director, as I see it, has been arbitrary, and in too many cases he has shown a cavalier disregard for the rights of these veterans. I hope the director now realizes that when members of parliament bring up these cases they do so with no political purposes in mind at all but in order to get action; and that these veterans are entitled to consideration of a different type from that which he has seen fit to show heretofore. I took no partin drafting the report of the public accounts committee; but, sir, that report shows not only that the committee was overwhelmed by the evidence given but also that when a serious situation is revealed action will be taken. To me one finding of the committee is one of the most strongly worded I have heard of, and I hope it will mean that hereafter, as far as the administration of the Veterans Land Act is concerned, sympathetic consideration will be shown by the minister, the deputy minister and the officials of that administration. This is a severe castigation, and it is the result of an accumulation of instances of injustice or arbitrary conduct. The committee came to the conclusion that they were not favourably impressed by the way evidence was given by an official, namely, the director. Without going into any individual cases I hope this will mean that no longer will any official feel that when cases are brought to his attention in connection with veterans he can

The demand has been made from this side of the house by the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Kamloops that a royal commission be appointed, but the government has indicated that it is opposed to that. If you continue in this haphazard way, while you may not be inviting other contractors who hitherto have been honest to do wrong, you certainly are penalizing them for doing right. I realize the difficulties in connection with a vast work of construction such as this. We are not asking for perfection, but we have a right to ask on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada that punishment follow wrongdoing.

I should like to make a few remarks in regard to the exchange situation and to ask the minister some questions. At the beginning, having seen the minister's experts sitting in the gallery for three days now, I am impelled to remark that they also serve who only sit and wait.
The day before yesterday was the day on which sterling officially became freely convertible; and I assume it is hoped this will greatly help our adverse trade position with the United States. I want briefly to look at the situation as it is represented in the public press, which is the only source of information available to me. According to that source, in the month of April we had an adverse trading balance with the United States of some $92-000,000, and it was estimated that our adverse balance of trade in May would approach or exceed $100,000,000. In addition we have a loss in investment capital of some $26,000,000 for the first four months of this year, In other words our adverse trading balance is running at the rate of approximately $1,000 million a year, and the direct capital loss is approximately $100 million a year. I think for the first time in our history at least since the first great war we had a net adverse balance
of trade on all counts, even assuming the free convertibility of sterling. In the first four months Canada had a favourable balance with the United Kingdom of $135 million; but with the adverse balance of trade with the United States of $296 million, assuming we could get payment for the United Kingdom balance in American funds it left us with a net deficit of $161 million in American funds. That is an extremely serious situation; for not only are we losing hard currency to the United States at a tremendous rate, but, on balance, we are not; even assuming the convertibility of soft currencies; meeting the adverse balance of trade.
Besides that our position is in debit with respect to capital, in that we are having our Canadian people invest larger sums in the United States than American citizens are investing in Canada-and that despite the apparent efforts of the foreign exchange control board.
Every modern war has been followed by increased prices. It was inevitable that there would be an inflationary trend after world war II, despite the fact that many programmes of control were put into effect to hold down prices. Since these stifled production in many instances, they encouraged rather than discouraged the inflationary trend, although they may have held it in check for a brief period.
This brings me to the point of considering the cost of government. I would compare this with the net cost of government in the United States, because I believe the economies of our two nations are so closely entwined that some comparison must be made. In 1939 the United States had a net government cost of some $10 billion and a national income of between $60 billion and $80 billion. The present estimated cost of United States government is around $50 billion per year, and the gross production of the country is, I understand, between $250 billion and $300 billion Therefore the ratio between cost of government and total net production of the country remains about the same, or approximately six to one. On the other hand, in Canada before the war, government cost us about half a billion per year while the national income was about $3 billion, or approximately the same ratio of six to one. Now the government cost in Canada is around $3 billion and, according to the last issue of the Canada Year Book, the national income is around $12 billion, making a shortage of production to the extent of about one-third. That is, the ratio of cost of our government to production is considerably greater than the ratio of cost of government to production in the United States.

The hon. member has

I have given before the reasons why we do not consider that Canadians should be permitted to export gold and sell it in these so-called free markets, and the reason of course is that we want to live up to our international obligations in that respect.
I would recall, first, that exports of gold from Canada have been controlled and licensed by the Minister of Finance under the gold export act of 1932, and this is not therefore a part of our wartime controls or a recent development. Under that legislation of 1932 it has been our policy in general to permit exports for sale in the normal monetary markets. In recent years, when premiums above that price existed in certain overseas markets, we have not granted licences for exports to those markets, for reasons I explained to the house before, and with which I believe those concerned are familiar.
It has also been our policy to grant licences for the export of certain gold-bearing concentrates or ores to the United States for smelting or refining, in those cases where proper facilities for economic smelting or refinement were not available in Canada, and that

Supply-Finance
applies to British Columbia. My hon. friend referred to concentrates or ores shipped to the American Smelting and Refining Company.
There are a few cases in which ores or concentrates of that kind contain arsenic. In the past the gold in these materials was paid for by the smelters or refiners in the United States on the basis of the standard price. According to press reports to which my hon. friend has referred, the American Smelting and Refining Company, which is engaged in this business, has recently announced its intention to market at premium prices the gold it produces from imported concentrates and ores, and has offered to pay ninety per cent of the premium to Canadian firms shipping gold-bearing material to them. In the past we have had no reason to concern ourselves with Canadian gold refined in the United States or being reexported from there at premium prices and therefore did not concern ourselves with its ultimate destination. I understand that the practice followed by the United States government is to require their own domestic producers to sell gold at the standard price but to place no restrictions on the reexport of foreign gold brought to the United States for refining. The United States government apparently feels as we do, that it is not wise to encourage international sales of gold at premium prices at this difficult and critical time. That was made quite evident in their official statement on June 24 endorsing the statement issued by the international monetary fund, in which the fund recommended to its members that they take effective action to prevent such transactions.
I presume the members of the committee have seen the statement on international gold transactions issued by the fund which was published by the United States government, but for those who may not have seen it I should like to read it:
The international monetary fund has given consideration to the international gold transactions at prices substantially above monetary parity which have been taking place in various areas of the world. Because of the importance of this matter the fund has prepared this statement of its views.
A primary purpose of the fund is world exchange stability and it is the considered opinion of the fund that exchange stability may 'be undermined by continued and increasing external purchases and sales of gold at prices which directly or indirectly produce exchange transactions at depreciated rates. From information at its disposal, the fund believes that unless discouraged this practice is likely to become extensive, which would fundamentally disturb the exchange relationships among the members of the fund. Moreover, these transactions involve a loss to monetary reserves, since much of the gold goes into private hoards rather than into central holdings. For these reasons,
the fund strongly deprecates international transactions in gold at premium prices and recommends that all of its members take effective action to prevent such transactions in gold with other countries or with the nationals of other countries.
It is realized that some of these transactions are being recognized by or through non-member countries or their nationals. The fund recommends that members make any representations whioh, in their judgment, are warranted by the circumstances to the governments of non-member countries to join with them in eliminating this source of exchange instability.
The fund has not overlooked the problems arising in connection with domestic transactions in gold at prices above parity. The conclusion was reached that the fund would not object at this time to such transactions unless they have the effect of establishing new rates of exchange or undermining existing rates of other members, or unless they result in a significant weakening of the international financial position of a member which might affect its utilization of the fund's resources.
The fund has requested its members to take action as promptly as possible to put into effect the recommendations contained in this statement.
That is the end of the statement. It was endorsed by the United States government on June 24. That is the reason why we believe it is in conformity with international obligations and in the public interest to prohibit exports of gold to this so-called free market.

It appears in a letter issued by the economics department of the Bankers Trust Company, New York, on June 13, 1947. It is entitled "The Canadian Exchange Situation." I will read only this one paragraph from the report:
On balance, the rise in the official Canadian exchange rate does not appear to have been responsible to any significant extent for the country's present exchange difficulties. Thus devaluation of the Canadian dollar, reversing the upward move of last year, would probably do more harm than good. It would bring little relief to Canada's present United States dollar scarcity and would not remedy the basic cause of the deficiency. On the other hand, the repeated manipulation of the official Canadian exchange parity would most likely have repercussions upon the long-term attractiveness of Canada for the investment of capital and would certainly harm the revival of orderly international monetary relations in which Canada herself is critically interested.

Whilst I realize that it is not popular to speak at any length at a time like this, I feel obliged to refer briefly to the serious international monetary situation, because I believe that it is being and has been aggravated by the financial policies of the western democracies. In this house attempts have been made by many people to sihow that we in this group are opposed to international trade and international cooperation. I doubt very much if there is any group in this house who believe to a greater extent in international cooperation than do the members of this group, but we believe that international cooperation must be on a basis of mutual advantage to all concerned and not on the basis of exploitation of the weaker nations by the larger creditor ones.
There has been a good deal of discussion about the united nations organization building for peace. I think we should realize that it is hopeless to try to build a temple of peace upon a foundation of economic war. When the minister spoke in the budget debate, he stated that our large adverse balance of trade with the United States was to a considerable extent the product of Canadian prosperity. Personally I would say it would be more realistic to say that it is the inevitable consequence of the international policies we have been pursuing and adopting since the war. For example, the scarcity of United States dollars existed prior to the war. During the war it was quite evident that this situation would exist after the war, even in an exaggerated state. But we took no steps to remove the cause of this deficiency. On the contrary we aggravated it and today we are reaping the consequences in a state of world financial chaos. I would say that the situation is very largely due to the failure of the western democracies to assume their full responsibility for the financial obligations [Mr. Abbott.!
arising out of the war, then to set their own house in order and be in a position to balance their own international payments.
In the past the great industrial nations have failed to provide their people with a purchasing power sufficient to maintain effective demand against their own production. Consequently these nations have invariably depended upon the export market to provide greater employment within their own borders. In other words, they have attemped to dump their unemployment problem on the doorstep of other nations. There is no doubt that the United States of America, when they put forward the Bretton Woods agreement, had that purpose in mind. I would say that was very largely the policy of the United States between the two wars. When I refer to the United States I want to make it clear that I am not in any way attacking the people of the United States. I have a high appreciation of those people. When I attack the international policy of the United States government I am no more attacking the people of the United States than I am attacking the Canadian people when I attack the foreign policy of the Canadian government. I do not think the people of the United States are responsible for their foreign _ policy, and certainly the Canadian people are not responsible for the foreign policy of this government. In many ways that policy is in spite of the people.
The international financial policy of the United States caused the great depression by drawing away the gold basis of other nations' ciirrencies, resulting in a general restriction of credit ; and the drastic trade restrictions and barter agreements were the result of that depression rather than the cause of it. I mention that fact because time and again we have had it pointed out by the Minister of Finance that we did not want the same kind of restrictions of trade that caused the depression. Those restrictions came into being after the depression and were the result of the depression, not the cause of it. They were as a result, as I say, of the gold basis being withdrawn from the nations' currencies, thereby forcing them to adopt a policy of currency and credit restriction. Today, unfortunately, instead of appreciating that situation and trying to take steps to force the creditor nations to carry out their responsibilities, we are continually and progressively stripping the weaker nations of their defences.
On March 8, 1944, the committee on reconstruction and reestablishment discussed the question of international currency plans and, generally speaking, what the post-war financial

position would be. At that time we had as a witness Doctor W. C. Clark. I wish to quote briefly from the record of that time. I will quote first from a statement I made and then the reply of Doctor Clark; this is at page 36:
*-if we are tying ourselves up to a proposal lin order to satisfy to a large extent the demands of the United States and such a proposal in the future brings about international friction, we are not going to help the situation very much. Today we recognize our responsibility in regard to providing goods to other nations in war time, and look upon it as a moral obligation. Doctor Clark points out that after the war there will be certain nations that will be unable to purchase imports; they will have neither foreign exchange nor exports with which to secure foreign exchange. That is true, and it seems to me that after the war for a number of years the same moral obligation that exists today to provide goods under the mutual aid or lease-lend schemes, goods which probably should be in the form of a gift, should exist for a number of years after the war in order to rehabilitate those countries that have been devastated as the result of the war. Fortunately we are in a geographical position where we are not suffering from that condition, but it is our moral obligation to help to restore the damage in these devastated countries just as much as it is to help win the war. 1 think that provision should be recognized and that instead of making loans we should make gifts of the necessary goods, and when those nations have become rehabilitated and have their industries restored and are able to produce, in a majority of cases those nations will be anxious to export goods in payment for their imports. So I think there is a clear-cut line there. First of all it is a question of rehabilitating nations and putting them on their feet so that they will be in a position to pay for imports with exports, and once that is accomplished I think our whole endeavour must be to devise a scheme whereby nations will 'be able to pay for their imports with exports.
Then I would like to quote from Doctor Clark's reply to that statement:
In the first part of his remarks, Mr. Quelch proposed a very idealistic solution of some of the early postwar-year problems. In other words, he suggested the continuation of mutual aid or of gifts to other countries which could not pay for their necessary imports.
Mr. Quelch:	Due to war devastation.
The Witness:	I take it he means very much
more in that connection than is implied by the UYRRA recommendations. That, as I say, is a fairly idealistic solution. If he could get that solution accepted by most of the countries of the world I would wish him a lot of success. I think, however, that you will find that even in wartime there is a considerable criticism of mutual aid to allied nations for assistance in the conduct of the war, and I would be rather fearful that it would be much more difficult to get acceptance of that solution by a great many countries of the world in the postwar period when the fervour of patriotism is not running so high amongst the peoples of the united nations.
You will notice, Mr. Chairman, that Doctor Clark referred to my proposals as being idealistic. In view of the events which have occurred since that time I think today people will agree that the proposals I put forward then were essentially realistic, because those are the very things that are being talked about as being necessary in order to restore confidence throughout the world. At that time Doctor Clark referred to UNRRA; but we must remember that initially UNRRA was regarded as a programme not merely of relief but of rehabilitation. Then it was amended under resolution 12 to become a straight relief project. I emphasized then that just giving people relief and continuing to keep them on relief would not permit them to get into the position where they could reconstruct their factories, rebuild their plant and rapidly get on their feet so they would be able to produce the goods needed to pay for the imports they would bring into the country. As I say, that was the discussion we had in 1944, and I repeat that I believe the stand took then, instead of being looked upon now as idealistic, must be regarded as the only realistic one. A statement in the Financial Post of May 24, 1947, fully substantiates that claim. On 'the front page we find an article written by Kenneth R. Wilson, which reads:
Great Britain has served notice that she foresees imminent economic catastrophe and a collapse of world trade. Basis of such a forecast is her belief that the world is running out of dollars.
As reported to me recently in Britain and indicated directly to high government authorities in Ottawa within recent weeks, British experts see Europe, Canada and herself directly involved in this expected breakdown.
If not averted, the pattern suggests world economic gloom and/or doom. It spells as well a breakdown of the multilateral system of trade and exchange on which Canada so largely depends. Such prognostications point essentially to the great economic question mark of our age: Will United States accept the responsibility of its post-war creditor position and match its vast productive surpluses with corresponding imports, loans or free gifts? All the world presently needs these surpluses but is going broke trying to buy them. Even Dean Acheson. retiring U.S. under secretary of state, said a few days ago that hope for world recovery lay in some new form of peace-time lend-lease by which United States could give away about $5 billions of goods annually.
Then he goes on to say:
Looking back on what has happened since war's end, and especially in the last six months, many well-informed people in Britain now believe the attempt towards multilateral trading and exchange has already broken down. They talk pessimistically about the world bank and the world fund as being "too little and too

During the Bretton Woods debate we pointed out the futility of relying upon the Bretton Woods agreement to bring about the reconstruction of the devastated areas of the world. Unfortunately the supporters of the Bretton Woods agreement refused to face that situation realistically. I emphasize the fact that if attempts were made to enforce Bretton Woods and the ancillary agreements it was bound to stir up international friction. Well, since that time the situation has become greatly aggravated ; and it is going to be far harder to deal with the situation now than if we had dealt with it in a realistic way immediately after the end of hostilities. Now, for instance, we have before us the Marshall plan. No one knows exactly what the Marshall plan stands for. When the estimates of the Department of External Affairs were before the house we tried to get the minister to tell us just what that plan was, and he implied that there really was no plan, though he also suggested that he had more information available than he was able to disclose. One thing is certain, however; the Marshall plan does mean some form of mutual aid or lease-lend or gifts to the stricken areas of Europe. Apparently today it is realized that the only way to bring about the recovery of the European countries is by some means of that kind.
I would say there is a real, sound justification for that stand. It may be remembered that during the war the allies pooled their resources for common use against the enemy. If every nation had cut down its standard of living to the bare necessities of life and made the rest of its resources available for war, then there should have been no question of debt as between the allies. But it may be remembered that before the United States came into the war Britain paid! that country six billion dollars in cash for ships, munitions and aircraft. Yet those ships, aircraft and so on were being used to defeat the enemy just as much as the ships and aeroplanes that were produced later on. One may well ask what would have been the consequence to the allies if Britain had waited for a Pearl Harbor before coming into the war. Yet those early expenditures by Britain had to be paid by herself, and were not put into the common pool.
Another thing that greatly aggravated the situation was that immediately after the day of- victory the United States cancelled lend-

lease; but unfortunately the costs of war do not end with the day of victory. The costs of war continue for many months and, in some cases years, after victory has been accomplished. So it was undoubtedly the obligation of the western democracies to absorb their full share of that cost, namely the cost of rehabilitating the devastated areas of the world.
That should have been clear in 1944. But when a person made that suggestion in 1944 he was branded as idealistic. I believe however it is recognized today that the suggestions we made in 1944 were most realistic. What happened instead of that? The United States made the price of further help first of all the acceptance of the Bretton Woods agreement, the reduction of the British preference and the policy of non-discrimination in trade. We in Canada supported the United States in that policy. Actually all we have done by that policy is to help develop the sphere of Soviet influence in Europe, because the people of Europe have no love for a reactionary laissez faire policy of capitalism. And as they could not get the help they believed they should get, naturally they turned more and more to the Soviet union. Now we find Great Britain indulging in discussions with the U.S.S.R. in the matter of a trade agreement.
I should like to say a few words about the Bretton Woods agreement and the United States charter for the expansion of world trade and employment. Both of these, it will be remembered, were sponsored by the United States, which country apparently was aspiring to a place of world leadership. When any nation aspires to the position of world leadership it is necessary to investigate its record in matters of that kind.
I should like first to refer to discussions which took place in the committee on banking and commerce with respect to Bill 238, when we had before us as a witness Mr. Rasminsky. I quote this from the proceedings at page 29 where Mr. Rasminsky states:

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Well, I had hoped, Mr. Chairman, that it would not be necessary to discuss at this late date in the session under existing climatic conditions the merits or demerits of the various Bretton Woods agreements, and I still entertain that hope. The international monetary fund, as I said a moment ago, was never intended to cover the whole field, and my hon. friend would be the first one to agree that the currency requirements of the European continent today are abnormal; they are not the normal ordinary balances which one would expect to meet under the old system, I suppose, of establishing gold. They are in large measure due to reconstruction requirements. The bank of reconstruction and development, as he knows as well as I do, was intended to provide some of that longer term capital. It is obvious that the requirements of these countries for reconstruction purposes are in excess of what these institutions can possibly provide; other and more direct means will no doubt have to be found, and that is what is involved in the discussions which are going on in Paris now, as my hon. friend knows, of what is called the Marshall plan. But I am not prepared nor can I today engage in a long and detailed exposition of what the fund or the bank is intended to accomplish. My hon. friend knows that that has been done on previous occasions. It may not accomplish its purpose, but this house has approved the participation of Canada in these two institutions, and we are going to see how they work out. That is the position. I have never been one who feels that there is a great deal of advantage in post mortems, particularly until we have given things a chance to work out.

I am not making a post mortem. I have suggested that if a certain situation arises we should have the right to make a recommendation to the fund. The minister says it cannot deal with everything. I agree. Surely it should not be allowed to act as an impediment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We have a right to make recommendations.

As I say, it should not be allowed to act as an impediment. Article VII states that when the currency of a nation
becomes scarce within the fund, restrictions on trade may be imposed. To all intents, United States dollars have become scarce. Why cannot the fund now declare United States dollars scarce so that any nation can feel absolutely free to impose restrictions on imports? Surely that is the logical thing. You could not have currency more scarce than United States dollars are today. Why cannot the fund declare United States dollars scarce? That is a logical question, as I think the minister will agree.

I feel, no doubt as do all hon. members, that superannuated civil servants, especially those who receive a small pension, are under great hardship in these times when the cost of living has risen to such a large extent. I think it is only just that this government should give consideration 'to these people who are underprivileged in these circumstances and who, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has said, sometimes receive much less than old age pensioners. This government should consider immediately giving to them the relief for which they are asking.

No individual or party has any monopoly on a desire to see fairness accorded to *the civil servants. I join in supporting what has been said, and I know something about it because my own father was a civil servant in the dominion service for many years. In that connection I would point out 'that one of the great difficulties about superannuation is this. Where over the years a person pays in to the fund and then passes away shortly after becoming entitled to be pensioned, the reduction in many cases by 50 per cent of the amount which was to foe paid so long as the civil servant and his wife continued to live often brings the amount so low as 'to make it almost impossible for the relict or the widow to live after the departure of the pensioner.
I want to bring two or three representations to the attention of the minister in connection with compulsory savings. This is a matter that affects hundreds of thousands of Canadians. During the period of the war it was almost impossible to keep clear and definite records as to who would be entitled to the return of the refundable portion or the compulsory saving after the war. Each year when income tax was paid the individual was given a slip indicating the amount of the refund

to which he was entitled. Well, untold numbers of those slips have been lost. In that connection there is this further point, that employees moved from one job to another, from one type of employment to another, with the result that today many have nothing to show that they are entitled to the refund of any amount. As a matter of fact in certain cases it is going to be almost impossible to identify the individuals concerned, if indeed they have not already passed on. I suggest one of the reasons the governor in council has not seen fit to provide for an earlier return of the amounts to which these people will be entitled is 'the tremendous wall of difficulty that will have to be scaled before these payments can be made. An analogy comes to mind in connection with the wheat board, which issued certificates in 1941, 1942 and 1943. Many of those certificates ran into large sums of money, but thousands have been lost, even including some for quite large amounts.
First I should like to place before the minister this suggestion. The first of these payments is 'to be made not earlier than March 31, 1948. I come in contact with people in all parts of the country, and they ask, "When are we going to get back this money? We have nothing to. show any longer. What is going to be done to protect us?" Would I be presuming if I were to suggest to the minister that now is the time to get ready for making the great bulk of the payments that will have to be made, and I suggest a series of advertisements or radio announcements now so that people will be able to establish their claims and the government will be in a position to meet the great volume that will come pouring in an avalanche within the next few months.

Mr. ZA-PLITNY: The fact of the matter is-and I shall give figures to support my contention-that the people of Canada are convinced the government has followed its decontrol policy much too fast, and with too much recklessness and with complete disregard for those in the low income groups.
1 shall begin by pointing out that as recently as July 15 of this year there appeared in the Winnipeg Tribune a report on a public poll on the question of price control. The question was asked whether in their opinion prices had been decontrolled too fast, not fast enough or more or less reasonably. When the minister spoke last year on his budget he referred to a national stabilization programme. That, sounded dramatic and high sounding, but I have yet to see any evidence of such a programme. The closest calculation I have been able to make is that the pre-war dollar of 1939 is worth no more than, sixty cents today. First of all, the so-called national stabilization programme promised over a year ago by the then minister of finance has not been followed out by the government, in spite of the fact that public opinion polls show definitely that the people in favour of such a programme were willing to support it and are Still in favour of it.
Second, I am pointing out the reasons why the cost of living has risen as sharply as it has. The reason quite definitely is not that wages have gone up because, according to the bureau of statistics, t'he average wages were lower in the first nine months of 1946 than they were in 1945. May I quote an authority which I think my hon. friends to the right will accept, the Financial Post. In one of its editorials, the Financial Post comments to the effect that there has been an "unexpected buoyance in corporation profits in Canada in 1946". I wonder why is was unexpected. Possibly the reason it was unexpected to the Financial Post itself was that the corporations themselves felt that the government was going to carry out its national stabilization programme which was promised to the Canadian people a year ago. They got more concessions than they had expected themselves, apparently.

But these figures are significant. In 1944 we were told that the consumption of milk was still twenty-five per cent below the minimum level of consumption

Hon. members know what the action of the government was. Subsidies were withdrawn. The price of milk has gone up, not the same across the country, but it has gone up sharply in most of the cities. The result is that the consumption of milk is again dropping. We have not yet reached the full point at which the consumption of milk could be considered adequate, but we are starting down hill again and it will not be long before we shall be starved for milk once more.
I want to point out also that when the then minister of finance spoke on the same day as I quoted earlier, he used these words:
The policy of paying subsidies will remain in effect in order to prevent undue increases in prices of articles of major importance in the consumer's cost of living and in primary producers costs of production.
That is a general statement, but if it means anything at all it must mean that the prices of the things that go into the cost of production will be held down by this government. I claim that that has not been done; and the indication now is, as was forecast in the papers only a few days ago, that by October of this year practically all the price controls will have been removed, with perhaps the exception of rent and sugar. That is not what the people of Canada expected, or were led to believe from the statements that were made by the former minister of finance in this house only one year ago. I want to make a protest-I consider it my duty to do so-on behalf of the farmers of western Canada, to whom the stabilization of prices in this country means more than it does to any other single occupation or group.
