There is a great deal of resentment today and, I think, legitimate resentment, on the part of the farmers, who feel that they have been led down the garden path by the present government. That is true, not only of the farmers themselves, but of the different classes of people who were mentioned by the minister himself. He referred to the incomes of primary producers, pensioners, teachers, office workers, and so on. One of the reasons why this session has lasted as long as it has is that we have debated hour after hour about doing something for this class of people, that class of people and the other. Why? Because the cost of living has gone up so much that today they are not able to make a living. Hon. members around me have been making a plea for the superannuated civil servants because the cost of living has gone up. Yesterday we heard a discussion about wartime housing and it has gone on today. We have been told that the cost of building these houses has gone up terrifically. Why? Because the price of the things that go into them has gone up, and so on. Practically all the problems that have been faced by this parliament during this session had as their underlying cause the fact that the price stabilization programme promised by the government a year ago has broken down, has not been carried out. I want to say frankly to the Minister of Finance that, in my opinion, he has been one of those responsible for the hatchet job that has been done on the price stabilization of this country. His political views are such that, to put it in plain words, he is, in my view, more reactionary than the former minister of finance was. Apparently he believes that the sooner we get back to this high and mighty sounding free enterprise economy, the better off we shall be. If he can show me how he can operate a free enterprise economy in fairness to all I shall be willing to listen. But here is something that is happening right now. This is a publication of the Department of Labour, the Labour Gazette of February, 1947. It points out that the annual report of the proceedings under the Combines Investigation Act was tabled on January 31, 1947. The report read in part as follows. This is a direct outcome of the sweeping away of controls.

The imminent or actual withdrawal of many governmental war-time restrictions led trade associations in a number of instances to consider the introduction of various forms of cooperative activity on a voluntary basis.
It sounds good up to that point, but what is this voluntary cooperation? The statement goes on:
Organized groups in several distributive trades were found to have in active preparation programmes of joint activity which included objectives such as the adoption of uniform selling prices and other restrictions on competition.
How will the minister square that kind of thing, the direct outcome of the free enterprise system, with the objective of the free enterprise system? Free enterprise is being destroyed by the very people who shout "free enterprise". They are combining themselves into monopolies and cartels and are restricting competition, setting prices where they want them, without regard to the law of supply and demand. Further on, the statement is more damning:
It became increasingly evident during the inquiry which was made into private business agreements that serious restraints on trade may develop out of arrangements which, in so far as they become apparent to the public, may bear an appearance of innocent protection of private interests but which when fully disclosed are found to be restrictive to an injurious degree.
There you have it quite plain in a. government publication warning the government as early as February of this year, while there were still considerable controls on, that forces were at work organizing for the purpose of restricting trade, forming monopolies and entering into agreements in order to set an artificial price far above the necessary level, and extracting from the people all the profits they can get. That has been and is still going on. apparently with the blessing of the present Minister of Finance.

Mr. BLA'CKMORE: We have had a very fine preparation for the serious consideration of the whole way of carrying on which we are following in our system, economic and financial. I 'believe everyone was greatly impressed when the matter of mutual aid legislation was being discussed by certain members. A good many members, I believe, wondered how in the world such a mutual aid contribution as $5 billion a year from the United States could be financed. The other day I was reading an article in a United States publication in which the author raised that question. He asked how long the United States economy could endure such a strain.
It is quite obvious that it would be good for the United States economy if she could get rid of those $5 billion worth of goods. She needs to do that, because, unless she sees how to get rid of her goods, she is unable to see how she can employ her people. Very much of the present questionable United States trade policy which is driving the nations almost into a frenzy of despair arises from the fact that the United States leaders feel instinctively that they must get rid of vast quantities of their goods abroad. They do not know how in the world to get rid of them, how they will be paid for.
This is a serious matter, because it goes to the heart of the whole economic situation confronting the world, and it could involve us in another ruinous war. One of the main difficulties with the United States is that she is unable to put her own people in a position to consume her goods. If she could do that she would not have to worry so much about ridding herself of goods outside. That is an important problem which must challenge the most earnest thought of every thinking person in the Anglo-Saxon world today, inside this parliament and out.
Another problem raised this afternoon rather incidentally is this one. Suppose the United States advances $5 billion worth of goods for a periodl of five years, $5 billion a year. She will have $25 billion worth of goods owed to her at the end of the five-year period. The nations that received those goods will be desirous of repaying, granted their economies have been rehabilitated at that time; but the
United States will be afraid to accept goods from those nations in return, lest those goods should compete ini her markets with her own goods. The result will be that the nations which received the $25 billion worth of goods will be eager to repay the United States; the United States will be eager to receive payment, but she will not be able to receive goods in return. The result will be another utterly confounding situation which will require some method of treatment different from anything we have applied in the world up to the present time.
I submit that this afternoon has been full of provocative expressions on the floor of the house and that the discussion has been very valuable. I doubt whether we have had a more profitable afternoon since I came to parliament this year. Lately the hon. member for Dauphin has been raising two problems that are not far from the minds of all hon. members; one of them has to do with prices. It is one thing to say that we want prices down and another to see how we shall get them down and keep them down.
The minister correctly said a few minutes ago that you cannot pass laws to keep prices down in peace time because people will not submit to them. At the same time you need to be able to keep prices down. If you are unable to do that, you lose the value of your money because the more prices rise, the more the value of the dollar declines.
Another serious problem which faces our generation throughout the world is the question of finding money to pay to the people who are needy, those in receipt of small pensions. That has been exercising us. There are members who have done their duty and have done it quite well by bringing to the attention of the government during the last few days the many liabilities that face the government, moral liabilities, the many things the government ought to do. But the most interesting fact is that none of these gentleman who have raised these questions concerning the things the government ought to do has made any suggestions as to where the government can get the money to do these things.
I trust that hon. members will indulge me if I endeavour to give some attention to the question as to how to get that money. Hon. members will, I am sure, at once say that I am going to talk about the printing press and the creation of money and they will say immediately, that is the old story; there is nothing to it. Well, I would ask hon. members is there anything to the ideas they have? Can they see in their orthodox way of thinking any conceivable way out of the

difficulty I have indicated? I think every hon. member will have to say frankly, "No, I cannot." Very well. When a person gets into that frame of mind, he ought to be receptive, anyway. So, Mr. Chairman, I think it might not be amiss to devote a certain amount of the valuable time of hon. members to a discussion of this most important problem. As you will remember, we spent thirteen hours in discussing the redistribution bill. I am not saying, that any one of those hours or any one of those minutes was unwisely spent. But if we can find any inkling of a solution to these desperate problems which face us, and which are so bewildering, I ithink the house would not be spending its time unwisely if it devoted thirteen weeks to the discussion of such a solution. One of the unfortunate things about our discussions in the house, since I have come here, is that so little of our time is devoted to finding a way out of our difficulties. So now I make bold to ask the indulgence of the members of the house while I go into this matter with some care.
During the war many people spoke of a new order. I think our own Prime Minister was one of the leaders in Canada who did so. Most people believe that a new order could be possible when they look at the machines we have, the solar energy we have learned how to use, the plastics we have learned how to create, and the unemployment which normally is everywhere around us, showing that we have a surplus of man-power as well as great quantities of materials. Everybody says, "Surely, if we have all the materials which evidently are available and all the man-power which evidently is available, there must be something wrong with us if we cannot have a new order of abundance where everybody can have at least all he needs". Eight into that situation when people had learned what I have already mentioned, there came a statement of Doctor Charles A. A. Stine, an eminent chemist in the United States, that between 1940 and 1942 they had discovered new continents of matter as a result of technological discoveries. He says that we have now between ten and one hundred times the raw materials at our disposal that we had in 1940. Then we had t'he breath-taking announcement of atomic energy, the possibilities of which no one today even dares to guess; for, if the atomic energy is of value in destruction, it must also be valuable in construction or building. There is no reason that I can see why we cannot learn to use atomic energy to accomplish many wonders which now would seem impossible. Those two 
discoveries, the discovery of plastics and the discovery of atomic power, open up to us matter and energy supplies which are literally limitless. I do not think any one of us has thought with much happiness about the possibilities of atomic energy applied to ordinary industry, because we think, "Well, if we learn how to use atomic energy instead of coal, look at what will happen to the coal miners. If we learn how to use atomic energy instead of gasoline, look at what will happen to all tlie gasoline purveyors," and so on, and so on, until most people would regard the matter, after a few moments' thought, with more than a little apprehension. That ought not to be. We are richer because we have discovered atomic energy. We are richer because we have discovered these new continents of matter.
It has got out into the minds of men, that somewhere between 1913 and 1928 the world had rounded a mighty corner and sped from an age of scarcity into an age of abundance. The better informed people have read such books as "Chart of Plenty", by Doctor Harold Loeb, published in 1936, which gave some information having an important bearing on the matter which the hon. member for Acadia was discussing a little w'hile ago and to which I have referred. What in the world will the United States do with all the goods she can produce? For this man pointed out that in 1935 the United States was able to produce so many goods that if she knew how to distribute them she could give $4,400 worth of goods to every family in the United States. All hon. members will recall what a pathetic situation the United States was in during 1935. There were 15,000,000 people unemployed. Only about twenty-one people out of every 100 were able to get the bare necessities of life. There was something desperately wrong there. What was it? Once more the challenge comes before us, what to do.
There are some citations which I should like to refer to once again, and which I have already mentioned, to show that the kind of thing I intend to talk about this afternoon is not entirely the work of the imagination of cranks or fantasts. The better informed people have read such books as "Economic Tribulation" by Vincent C. Vickers of the Vickers-Armstrong Company in England, who was at the same time a director of the Bank of England. This man almost with his dying efforts, wrote a book which was published in 1941, called "Economic Tribulation", in which he gave in considerable detail what he thought would happen if we did not have some changes. He talked about the destruction of the British empire, and the destruction of practically everything we hold

dear. Then he went on in his last chapter to suggest what he conceived to be the changes we needed, and1 these changes are singularly similar to the suggestions which the social credit movement has been making now for twelve years in this house and in various parts of the country.
Mr. Vickers was certainly not a social credi-ter, He thought his way to the conclusions he arrived at with his own knowledge and his own intelligence. I should now like to read, if I may just at this point, a little, quotation from a man whose opinions can hardly be too lightly disregarded.. I refer to the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna, chairman of the Midlands Bank in England. This man has said, in a report to his shareholders, that money can be created by the authorities themselves if they choose to exercise their power. He goes on to say that the age which produced all this wonderful skill in creating goods and creating power has also given us the means whereby to use those goods and that power without destroying ourselves. These are his words, which appear in the January 30, 1936, issue of the London Times at page 23:
Additional currency, however, can now he furnished by the authorities, if they choose to exercise their powers, without reference to the *central hank's holding of gold. _ Thus, the nineteenth century which brought into general use a means of payment hitherto scarcely known outside London, brought also the machinery whereby it could be subjected to intelligent control.
I believe in the truth of what the Right Hon. Reginald McKenna declared in those words. I believe they constitute a standing challenge to every public servant in the Anglo-Saxon world. The question we now want to have answered for ourselves is whether, if the authorities themselves create additional currency, that additional currency will be sound. Apparently we feel that additional currency will be sound enough if it is to be lent by banks out into circulation. What we all want to know is whether that currency would be sound if it were created by the government and spent into circulation without being borrowed from the bank and without being paid as wages to people working in industry. As soon as we can have those questions answered, we shall be in a position to appraise the whole concept which underlies social credit.
There will be those, I believe, who will read the words I am about to utter, in places that I cannot at present conceive. I should like to say what I am going to say in such a way that it will help them follow through the reasoning. I have selected a number of questions which, I believe, will help anyone
who follows them through to form an opinion as to the soundness or unsoundness of the proposal to have money created by the state and spend that money into circulation, provided that the amount of money created is not too great. I am going to read the questions. I may say I have put a copy of these questions in the hands of the authorities, so that they have had a chance to give thought to the answers. I do not believe they will have had time to prepare complete answers. Therefore I have endeavoured to answer the questions myself in many cases, and all the minister will have to do is question the answers I leave, which, I believe, will save the time of the committee and give us something rather constructive to work upon. I am going to start with a statement by the Prime Minister which is familiar to everyone:
Once a nation parts with the control of its currency and credit, it matters not who makes the nation's laws. Usury, once in control, _ will wreck any nation. Until the control of the issue of currency and credit is restored to government and recognized as its most conspicuous and sacred responsibility, all talk of the sovereignty of parliament and of democracy is idle and futile.
I have the following questions I should like to ask the minister:
1.	How would the minister define the expression "control of the issue of currency and credit" as used by the Prime Minister in this quotation?
I am going to leave that for the minister, because obviously it is his question to answer.
2.	Does the minister believe that the government of Canada at the present time has adequate control of the issue of currency and credit?
I would say the answer there is, no. The minister may question what I say, but that is my answer for reasons which I set forth in the following questions.
2.	(a) In the minister's opinion, what factors ought to determine the optimum desirable amount of money in circulation in a state?
The answer would be, I would say, in the words of Hon. C. A. Dunning, "the needs of business," and the needs of business, I would say, are the needs of production and consumption. or distribution. If the minister disagrees with that answer he may tell us why.
3.	Is adequate control of the issue of currency and credit being exercised in Canada at present by the Department of Finance? In other words, is the optimum desirable amount of money being maintained in Canada today?
My answer is, no. Consequently I would say that the objective the Prime Minister set for himself in 1934 has not yet been attained. One of the reasons I am asking this question now is to find out how to attain it.

3.	(a) If not, in what respect or degree is the Department of Finance falling short of the desirable objective?
I would say it is failing to get adequate production and failing to get adequate consumption. I think about all one has to do in order ito impress upon hon. members the fact that we are not getting adequate consumption is to read this little quotation, which I think I will take time to read now. This is an excerpt from a letter from the bureau of statistics addressed to myself and dated September 25, 1946. I read the third paragraph :
The percentage of wage-earners earning less than $450 for the twelve months' period prior to the date of the census, June 2, 1941, was 32-9 per cent; 28-7 per cent of the wage-earners reported earnings between $450 and $949; 29-9 per cent earned between $950 and $1,949, and 6-8 per cent earned $1,950 and over. 1-7 per cent of the wage earners did not state the amount of earnings for the year.
That letter is signed by Mr. J. L. Forsyth. I believe it was the hon. member for Dauphin who said it was stated that a man and wife and three children, if I remember correctly, required at least SI,800 a year in order to maintain a reasonable standard of health and decency in Canada at the present time. If that is correct, then this statement by Mr. Forsyth indicates that only 6-8 per cent of all the wage-earners in Canada in 1941 were receiving enough to provide for themselves a reasonable standard of health and decency. Surely no one will say that a system which could do no better -than this in 1941, the second year of the war, is getting enough purchasing power or currency and credit into circulation.
3. (b) And if not, what reasons would the minister give for any deficiency at present obtaining in the control of the issue of currency and credit in the conduct of Canada's financial and economic system?
I would answer that in this way. Inability to provide for most of the wage-earners of Canada an income which will enable them to buy the needs of life, which will enable them to buy the things Canada is able to produce in abundance; which means that, even though Canada may be able to produce great quantities of goods, she is unable to consume those goods in Canada. In other words, Canada will be in the same position as the United States; she will be seeking external markets in order to provide employment for her own pepole, and therefore she will be supporting the policies of the United States, the most favoured nation clause and all the rest of it. I believe that constitutes sufficient justification for the answer I gave to question 3 (b).

4.	In the minister's opinion what ought to be the definition of the expression "money in circulation?" Ought it to be the amount of money in possession of citizens of the state or the amount in the possession of the probable producers and consumers of the state?
I would answer that it is the latter. In addition I would say that one sees altogether too great a tendency on the part of people in Canada who study matters of this sort to look at the bank deposits and say that is the amount of money in circulation. That is not the amount of money in effective circulation at all. The amount of money in effective circulation is the money going into the hands of would-be producers to enable them to produce, and that which is going into the hands of the would-be consumers to enable -them to consume. All other money is more or less dead.

My answer would be yes, and I do not think the minister will question that.

I make this little statement because I had the matter up with the deputy minister of finance and other officials as well as the minister himself. Last December the manager of the J. W. Windsor Company of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island,

made application to the government for sugar under the following circumstances. This firm had been large buyers of cranberries in Prince Edward Island, and were shipping these cranberries for counter sale to Montreal, Toronto and other places. One of their shipments was frost-bitten, whether in transit I do not know, and they were not allowed to put those berries out for counter sale, because they were perishable. Consequently the cranberries were put in cold storage and the company made application for a quota of sugar to turn these berries into cranberry sauce. As the minister knows, cranberry sauce is made from cranberries, sugar and water.
The matter was taken up and referred from one department to another. Finally the sugar controller, someone in Montreal, said no, notwithstanding the fact that in 1944, under the very same conditions, some eight tons of sugar were allocated to this firm for the processing of cranberries. No legitimate reasons were given by the controller, who seems to have control of the finance department in reference to sugar. Now this man has to take a loss of from $4,000 to $5,000 if he dumps these berries, and as a young man in business that loss is too great for him to take. At the present time there is a big demand in the maritime provinces for cranberry sauce. You will find it in all the stores there, brought in from the Boston canneries; it is all imported. If the Boston canneries can obtain all the sugar they wish for processing, and since the two countries are supposed to be a unit in this regard, I cannot see why this firm of
J.	W. Windsor should be refused this sugar by the controller after a similar request was granted two years ago. As I say, it was impossible to get any logical reason as to why the request was refused; in fact there was only one conclusion that could be reached, and that was that they were dealing with a bunch of men who made no use of their heads for anything but common hatracks. I should like to ask two or three questions about the beet sugar policy of the country. The government's management of the beet sugar industry in Canada during the last ten years has left much to be desired. Perhaps in the last year the government's policy in this respect has been more reprehensible than during any other year. The result of it all has been that during the war t'he government managed to deprive Canadians of considerable quantities of sugar they might as well have had *the use of, and managed to lose for Canada a substantial amount of national wealth. Canadians are now in a position where they must pay $28 million during 1947 in United States dollars for sugar which is being imported from non-British countries. In addition to that, they have the beet sugar industry as a whole in a position in which, should we have a war, we would be in grave danger of being cut off from supplies which we would need to support our ordinary standard of living. ,
I consider those four misdeeds of the government are more than serious. In my judgment tire present sugar administrator has been a sabotaging influence on the Canadian beet sugar industry ever since he assumed the position he now holds. I now wish to go into some detail to demonstrate that fact.
In 1946 the sugar administrator granted sixty and three-quarter cents per hundred pounds of beet sugar to the beet growers. This was far too low a subsidy; it should have been much higher than that. In 1947 the sugar administrator granted a further sixty-four and one-quarter cents per hundred pounds, again far too low.
Mr. Sulkers, president of the Manitoba beet growers association, argued on January 27 that the 1947 increase should 'have been S1.08 instead of sixty-four and one-quarter cents. Mr. Sulkers was estimating the price, as near as he could, from the cost of raw which it was expected the sugar administrator would be buying from British and non-British countries. That is, Mr. Sulkers was arguing that the total dominion subsidy for 1947 should have been S1.68J, considering the estimated cost by the administrator of British and non-British raw.
After obtaining more accurate information as to the cost of general tariff sugars, the

Supply-Finance
delegation which met the sugar administrator in January were all agreed that $1.08 was still below parity. The reason for that was that Mr. Noble stated that he estimated the British West Indies 1947 sugar would cost eighty-five cents per 100 pounds more than the 1946 British West Indies sugar; and that general tariff sugars in 1947 would cost more than a dollar more than the 1946 general tariff sugars.
Mr. Noble refused to take the cost of general tariff sugars into the calculation, because he stated that before the war Canada had not had to import such sugar. I should like to speak for a moment or two on this general situation. For many years in Canada the price paid for beet sugar has been governed by the price which had to be paid for raw sugar from non-British countries and raw sugar from British countries. The two were taken together, considering the cost laid down at Canadian ports, the freight, the cost of refining and all other costs entering into production. Then the beet sugar price was fixed in accordance with the combined prices of empire raw sugars and non-empire raw sugars.
Mr. Noble in 1947 took the stand that he should not take into consideration the cost of non-British sugars. He insisted that the price paid for beet sugar should be on a parity with the price paid for only British empire sugar. This was a serious blunder, and I do not believe it was accidental. I shall read one or two quotations to show that what I have said is correct in respect of the way in which the price on beet sugar was arrived at in years past.
In the Ontario sugar beet producers association's submission on February 26, 1947, in paragraph 4, commencing at the seventh line and speaking of the price, they say:
That figure is arrived at by taking the average laid down cost of imported raw sugar from all sources, adding thereto the normal statutory duty of $1.29 per one hundred pounds and further adding the spread or margin allowed to the cane refiners, which currently we understand is $1.57 per hundred pounds. This was the basis upon which 'beet sugar in Canada was sold for many years pre-control, and surely is unassailable from my viewpoint since it was adhered to through a number of changes in the government and was never even challenged.
I shall read one more statement from beet sugar producers to demonstrate the truth of what I have said in respect of the method of determining the price of beet sugar. At page 3 of a document called "Notes on the Dominion Subsidy on Domestic Sugar Production," prepared by the delegation which waited on Mr. Noble on January 27, 1947, we find this:
For many years pre-war, in fact probably from the inception of the beet sugar industry in Canada, beet sugar was sold at a price which was practically the same as the price (at any given point) which could be obtained by the cane sugar refiners for their sugars. (There was a slight differential of five cents to eight cents per hundred pounds against beet sugar.) The cane sugar price was made up of the following components: first, the laid-down price of raw sugars imported from all sources (including freight), plus the normal general tariff duty of $1.29, plus the refiners' margin or spread. This was the basis on which the beet sugar in Canada was sold and it is considered unassailable from any viewpoint, since it was adhered to through a number of changes in the government and was never challenged.
Those two statements by men who were in the beet sugar industry for many years should carry a tremendous amount of weight. But those contentions were disregarded by the sugar administrator in 1947, and apparently in previous years. The chairman of the Canadian Sugar Beet Producers Association in a letter of March 6,1947, asked for $1.02 per 100 pounds more, instead of the 641 cents, which would raise the total subsidy in 1947 to $1.66 per 100 pounds.
I have Mr. Baker's letter; perhaps I should read a portion of it into the record. Mr. Baker says:
We further request that the benefit payment increase on sugar beets for 1947 granted by the W.P.T.B. be raised from $0.64J to true parity as outlined above, which is $1.66 per 100 pounds of white sugar.
I am not saying that Mr. Baker is absolutely right in his calculation, because the beet producers do not all agree as to what the price should be, but they are all certain that it should be far more than what was granted them. I am certain of that too.
Mr. Baker is a big beet producer.

Yes, he is president of the Canadian organization of the sugar beet producers. As I have said, the contention of the beet producers is that the price of the nonempire sugars and the price of the empire cane sugars should be combined to form an average upon which the price of beet sugar should be based. It is at this point that the difficulty has arisen, and I want to give the minister a chance to explain. According to the information which I have from these gentlemen, the duty paid price of raw sugar imported into Canada pre-war was the same for sugar from empire sources as from foreign countries,

The British West Indies sugars had had a duty of $1.29, and a dollar had been allowed to empire producers as empire preference. That dollar had been given to the empire producer in whatever island the sugar came from. This is no longer done, but the duty on empire sugars should be exactly the same as the duty on non-empire sugars; that is, SI.29. When that fact is established and borne in mind and accepted, then the computation is as I have indicated. The price of cane sugar refined should be $8.02, and that means that the price of beet sugar refined should be $8.02.
Instead of this, these are the returns allowed for beet sugar in 1947: Ceiling wholesale refined, list price Montreal, net $4.89; reduction of excise tax, on sugar $1.00; total beet subsidy for 1947 crop, $1.25, which includes various items which the minister knows about and which I shall not mention. This brings the total price allowed for beet sugar to $7.14. It should be obvious to any hon. member that if cane sugar refined costs $8,02 and beet sugar is allowed only $7.14, then beet sugar is deprived of 88 cents of what it should have in order to have a parity. That point is exceedingly important to the beet sugar industry in Canada this year.
I am going to follow this a little farther. According to a bulletin from Czarnikow Limited of June 12, 1947, raw sugars from the British West Indies have been reduced, while imports from Cuba and Santo Domingo have been speeded up by 100,000 tons. These extra general tariffs at $4-925 (United. States currency), f.o.b. the islands, will greatly increase the proportion of general tariffs and considerably increase the cost of cane sugar this year. This would raise the parity price increase of beet sugar still further beyond what had been granted.
It is quite obvious that there is something .seriously wrong with the way in which Canada -is treating her beet sugar industry. I should 
like to show hon. members what other countries are doing for their beet sugar industry, for instance, Great Britain and the United States. I am reading from the British Sugar Beet Review of June, 1947, page 121, as follows:
Announcement of a new increase in the United Kingdom beet price makes British payments for 1947 the highest of those offered by the "Big Three" members in the international sugar pool.
The British government has added five shillings (about $1.20 at par) to the 1947 price for a long ton of sugar beets. This is the second increase given for this year's crop, and brings the price to over $21 per short ton of sugar beets of 15J per cent sugar content (exchange at par).
(Reason given for this extra payment is the concentration of delayed work undertaken by the farmers, the extra expense, and the risk of reduced yields-all caused by the late spring.
May I pause right there to point out to hon. members the contrast between what Great Britain has done for her beet producers and what the Canadian government have done for the producers in this country. There are people in Canada who did everything in their power to get the government to give even slight consideration to the beet sugar industry this year. Even when Ontario was having a wet spring, it was impossible to get any move whatsoever from the Canadian government. That attitude simply does not compare favourably with what the British are doing. I quote:
The United States government has guaranteed to growers a national average of $14.50 per ton of beets with 16-2 per cent sugar content. In Michigan the best producers' return will be almost $16.
While the Canadian government does not guarantee a floor price, present sugar ceiling prices will give Ontario growers $12.11 per ton of 16-2 per cent sugar beets. Inclusion of the Ontario subsidy will improve this figure, but sugar beet prices in Ontario will still lag behind those of Michigan and United Kingdom by approximately $3 and $8 respectively.
I should like to know and I think the people of Canada have a right to know just how it is the Canadian government seems to feel that it is justified in kicking the beet sugar industry around. Why is it that the government can find no value in the beet sugar industry? Beet sugar in Canada is just as valuable as any other kind of sugar, just as valuable as it is in the United States, especially when we are buying raw cane sugar from Cuba and other non-British countries and paying United States dollars for it. This year we are probably paying $28 million, as I indicated a moment ago, and we cannot afford to spend this money in that way. The fact that we are doing this is another bit of evi-

Supply-Finance
dence that there is something radically wrong with the Canadian way of dealing with the beet sugar industry. One would imagine that the people in the administration had not cut their wisdom teeth at all.
I wish to point out two or three matters which I think need special clarification by the minister. I do not suppose the minister will remember all these things, because he is a very busy man. In order to recall to him some of the things that he has said and written, may I read an excerpt from a letter which he wrote on March 19, 1947, to Mr. Philip Baker, chairman of the Canadian Sugar Beet Growers Association of Lethbridge, Alberta. In the .third paragraph of that letter the following words appear:
In reply may I say that the policy of the wartime prices and trade board has been to assure the producers of sugar beets a return equivalent to the 1 fjid down duty paid cost of preferential sugars.
I am going to stop there, and I shall have more to say about that later on. On what authority and under what justification did the wartime prices and trade board lay that down as a policy? That policy had not prevailed in Canada before. All the time in Canada before, the price of beet sugar had depended upon the sugar imported from British preferential countries and from non-British countries; when the war broke out, when people having anything resembling common sense would know that we ought to be able to produce sugar to the utmost of our capacity, because of the exigencies of the situation, the wartime prices and trade board had to make a ruling of this sort!
The minister goes on and says this:
Traditionally, Canada never bought any full-duty sugars for domestic use; such full duties as were purchased in pre-war years were invariably for re-export as refined.

Whoever gave the minister that lie committed a serious offence. That is quite clear. I have figures which will establish the statement I have just madie.

Then, to show the basis for what I have said, I am going to read to the committee the imports from non-empire countries and the total exports in each year. The stand the sugar administration took, the stand the minister takes, and the stand the Minister of Justice took in what he said on April 22, 1947, is this, when the sugars were imported from non-empire countries they were imported to be refined and reexported again for sale. Let us see. In 1916, 282.053,935 pounds of sugar were imported from Cuba, San Dominican Republic and other non-empire countries, and the total export of sugar that year was 629,274 pounds; in other words, 400 times as much sugar was imported from non-empire countries as was exported by Canada. Therefore 1916 does not bear out the statement of the minister, does it? In 1917, 280,342,992 pounds were imported from non-empire countries, and 57,788,131 pounds were exported. Therefore we have five times as much sugar imported from nonempire countries as was exported altogether from Canada.
In 1918, 450,220,719 pounds were imported from non-empire sources and 136,945,375 pounds were exported. That is three times as much sugar was imported from non-empire countries that year as was exported altogether. In 1919, 509,348,320 pounds were imported from non-empire sources and 2,052,935 pounds were exported; that is 250 times as much sugar was imported from non-empire countries as was exported altogether.

It is obvious that in every single year, from 1916 down to 1939 when the war broke out, the statement of the minister in that letter is proved to be completely false. As I said, the minister is not responsible but someone supplied him with false information.

It (beet sugar production) could be driven up further and the imports from empire countries-they are mainly from empire countries, certainly in time of peace-can be pressed down if we want to spend enough money to do it.

Once more there is complete fabrication, falsification evidently emanating from the same source that the misstatements given by the two ministers had emanated from.
Mr. Noble's statement to the joint delegation of the Canadian beet growers association and the beet sugar processors of Canada I will read into Hansard. This is from notes of that interview prepared by both the producers and processors and signed by responsible officials representing both. Here is the statement:
He-
Speaking of Mr. Noble, on page 2.
-stated that pre-war Canada had not had to import such sugars.
Of course he may have a way out there when he says she had not had to do so, but I am not sure about that. Certainly the impression he tried to give was that Canada had never imported non-empire sugars for Canadian domestic use. Once more there is complete falsification. All these four statements must have originated with the sugar administrator, S. R. Noble. They prove that man to be either culpably ignorant or downright dishonest. The obvious object of his mendacity has unquestionably been to cheat the beet sugar industry out of a considerable share of money to which it was entitled. In other words, his object was to discriminate against the beet sugar industry.
The Minister of Finance, in his letter on March 19, 1947, to Philip Baker, said:
The policy of wartime prices and trade board has been to assure the producers of sugar beets a return equivalent to the laid-down duty paid cost of preferential sugars.
I submit that when the sugar administrator laid down that policy for determining the price to be paid to the producers of beet sugar he committed a crime of discrimination against the beet sugar industry. Hon. members will recall that when we were discussing this matter on April 22 and the Minister of Justice was defending Mr. Noble, the Minister of Justice said, at page 2285 of Hansard:
I see no evidence whatever of any discrimination on the part of Mr. Noble against the beet sugar industry. I regard Mr. Noble as one of the best public servants in Canada.
It is astonishing how a man of the intelligence of the Minister of Justice can be so deceived, is it not? By laying down that rule, the sugar administrator precluded the possibility of paying fair prices to the beet sugar producers in war time. No man with any sense will fail to know that during war time there were a great many difficulties that do not exist in peace time. It would be hard to
get labour and materials; the cost would be more. There would be many difficulties increasing the cost of production. And yet, by tieing ithe price of beet sugar to the cost of sugar from empire countries alone, the islands where they produce cane sugar, he rendered it impossible for him to give a price which would allow for increased costs of production, a price which would stimulate production in Canada, as production ought to be stimulated.
On both these scores I think the sugar administrator deserves the roundest kind of condemnation. By laying down that rule, he paved the way to more flagrant abuses and soon followed that rule by an act of perfidy natural to a man who would draft the first rule. Effective on April 1, 1942, he caused all tariffs or duties against cane sugar entering Canada to be abolished by order in council P.C. 6582 of July 27, 1942, retroactive to April 1.
It may be said that the sugar administrator had nothing to do with the passing of the order in council. Well, if he was administering sugar I presume he had a good deal to do with the cabinet. The cabinet was acting probably on the advice of the Department of Finance, which was acting on the advice of the trade board, which was the tool of the sugar administrator as regards sugar. The normal duties on raw cane sugar have not been restored, and this is another astonishing thing. The duties against sugar entering the United States and Britain have been restored. We are entering the third year after the war; at least we are. closing the second year after the close of the war and still these duties have not been reimposed. What does it mean? Does it mean that under a smoke-screen or behind a smoke-screen of war conditions it is the intention of the government or .the Department of Finance to remove the tariff protection behind which the beet sugar industry has functioned? Has their determination to destroy the beet sugar industry in Canada driven them as far as .that sort of injustice?
The Minister of Justice, in his remarks on April 22, was extremely offensive in his insinuations against the beet sugar industry. He spoke there as though the beet sugar industry, in receiving some sort of tariff protection, was receiving something to which it had no possible title whatever. In this connection I believe it would be interesting for the people out in the country, in reading Hansard, to know how well we protect all kinds of vegetables in this country. There has been a reprehensible attempt on the part of the government authorities in the Dominion of Canada to destroy the beet sugar industry. been told and spread over the country trying to discredit the beet sugar industry, talking about salt fish and all that kind of thing. They tell one lie just as long as they can get away with it, to use a common expression, and then get another one.

Mutton, 4 cents a pound British preferential tariff, 8 cents a pound general tariff and 6 cents a pound intermediate tariff. Oats. 16 cents a bushel general tariff and 9 cents a bushel intermediate tariff. Peaches, 20 per cent general tariff and 15 per cent intermediate tariff. Let us hear no more, Mr. Chairman, from anyone who desires to tell the truth in this country disparaging tariff protection on the beet sugar industry, with the implication that the industry has no right to have tariff protection; and if it does have tariff protection then it has no right to exist in Canada. That seems to be the idea behind some of these remarks and it is just about time it was stopped.
I now go on to another aspect of the question. The removal of these tariffs against cane sugar coming into Canada is estimated to have cost the Canadian people between April 1, 1942 and December 31, 1946, $25,035,871.98. That would be the duties at preferential rates on empire sugars and the duties on general tariff sugars if they had been charged

the regular duty all during these years. I am not saying it was not a good policy to remove those tariffs. It might have been quite all right. But the point is that just as soon as they removed those tariffs they gave the sugar administrator absolute authority to charge the cane producers whatever he chose, giving almost complete discrimination in favour of -them and giving complete discrimination against beet sugar producers. The way was clear now for the sugar administrator to fix arbitrarily the price he would charge the cane refineries for raw cane sugar. He fixed that price at $4.32 per hundred according to my information. This put him in position to discriminate in favour of cane refiners on an extensive scale which I take it was the reason he was put there; while by his rule for fixing price of beet sugar he had placed himself in position to discriminate against-beet sugar producers, which I take it was the second reason he was put there. He then had to accumulate a considerable stabilization fund to enable him to absorb 'the shock and keep the consumer's price from rising. We will grant that he has done that well, but what price has been paid for it? The Canadian people ought to know this because it cost $25,000,000 in their taxes or in other revenues to keep the prices stable. Prices can be kept stable with a substantial fund like that to accomplish t'he objective. The sugar administrator levied 29 cents per hundred from April 1, 1942 which was to be collected from the Canadian refineries. He adopted other means also whereby he built up a considerable fund. He managed to conceal from the people the mischief he was making in the Canadian economy.
I have very little more to say and what I do say takes the form of certain suggestions which I believe will have something to do with the sugar administrator and certain others. First of all I recommend to the government that the control of the Canadian sugar supply has been committed to the mischievous clutches of a gang of saboteurs who have been striving to mismanage the beet sugar industry to death. I recommend that -the government forthwith rescue the valuable Canadian beet sugar industry from -the malicious grasp of this gang of self-seeking racketeers and turn the industry over to the Minister of Reconstruction or some other man who has sense enough to recognize a national asset when he sees one, and who has public spirit and honour enough to seek to provide for Canadians their needs of vital sugar supplies in the years to come. I recommend that at a very early day the Canadian government make Mr. S. R. Noble ambassador to China or Japan or some other
place far enough away to keep him from further exercising his malignant influence on the Canadian economy.
Mr. MacNI-COL: Would Timlbuetoo be a good place to send him?

I would suggest -that the beet sugar producers be called together to decide what price should be paid in order to stimulate the production of beet sugar in this country, so that it will supply at least thirty per cent of the Canadian consumption. It would be a most pleasant change-they say variety is the spice of life, and this would be a most pleasant variety-to call the beet sugar producers together for once and let them have a voice in dictating the policy with respect to sugar in Canada.
Now, Mr. Chairman, I trust that from this time forward the Canadian people will become so aroused that no longer will they tolerate this tampering with an exceedingly valuable industry. Let it be known that next time we shall have a super-global war. We had a global war this time; we shall have a superglobal war next time, and who can say that if that time comes we are going to have access to the empire countries which are producing sugar? Would it not 'be of tremendous value to the economy of Canada and the economy of the whole British commonwealth if we had in this country a beet sugar industry capable of producing all the sugar we need? Certainly the Canadian economy is completely capable of producing all the sugar we need and, indeed, of producing enough sugar to supply people in other countries which cannot produce sugar. I trust that greater wisdom will reign in the councils of this nation with regard to sugar.

I have just one question in connection with this matter. According to the latest reports from the bureau of statistics, this year Canada has on hand 35,344.000 pounds of sugar more than we had a year ago. On June 14, 1947, according to the record I have, the raw and refined sugar in Canada was 272,197,000 pounds, while on June 14, 1946, the figure was 236,852,000 pounds. Has the minister any additional information to give the committee to the prospect of any increase in the ration.
Then I wish to join with what has just been said by the hon. member for Lethbridge in regard to the need of encouraging beet sugar production in this country. In the United States a new sugar act has been adopted within the last few days by the -house of representatives, and apparently no difficulty is anticipated in having it adopted also by the senate. Under that legislation the United States beet sugar industry will be assured of

I ask the minister whether or not it is intended in Canada to follow the lead of the United States in this regard, and encourage an increase in the production of beet sugar in this country. I point out that in 1947, according to the statistics I have before. me, Canada will require $28,000,000 in United States currency for raw sugar imported from Cuba and Santo Domingo; and with the shortage of United States dollars to which the minister referred today, and' with very little hope that this shortage will become any less during the next year, I ask whether it would not be a wise economical course to endeavour to encourage the production in Canada of as large a share as possible of our sugar consumption. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
In point of fact, we have given encouragement to sugar beet production in Canada, and I am advised that 1946 showed a greater increase in beet sugar production in this country, as compared with pre-war, than in any other beet sugar producing country in the world. That is the actual position. Of course there is no doubt an increase in the production of beet sugar would have to be at the expense of some other field crops.
On the question of the sugar stocks, it is true they are slightly higher than last year, but not higher than normal. I have before me a chart which shows that our normal sugar stocks at this time of year, and the stocks we have now are not above normal. It so happens that we had larger importations of Cuban sugar, I think it was, in the last month or two than we had at the same time last year, which accounts for the temporary increase in the sugar stocks on hand. As to the prospects for any increase in the sugar ration, I have nothing to add to the statement I made not so long ago.

I wish to make a few remarks under this item in reference to the government policy of paying subsidies on feed grain shipped from western Canada to the eastern provinces. I particularly wish to refer to a remark made by the hon. member for Melfort. I am sorry the hon. gentleman is not in his seat at the moment, but his statement was as follows:
The minister had a word to say with regard to the increased production of pork. He admits that this increase is in eastern Canada, and that it is due to the assistance given by way of freight rates and subsidies on feed grain to the east. I have maintained that the increase in production in eastern Canada is not economic. It is costing the government of this country $3 for every hog produced in eastern Canada, through freight assistance and subsidies on feed grain. That pork should be produced in western Canada, where the grain is grown. That is where you can get the most economic production of pork and poultry products in Canada; and until we get an agricultural policy under which we shall have economic production we shall not be able to compete in the world markets; we shall not be able to give our own people food

Supply-Finance
at an economic price; and until we change our policies so that we can do these things we shall not be any better off.
The hon. member states it is not economically sound for the government, to pay subsidies on feed grains shipped from the west to the eastern provinces, and to pay freight rates from the head of the lakes on that grain. He states that pork and poultry should be produced in western Canada where the grain is grown.
We have to pay subsidies on western coal, and we are glad to pay them.

The fact of the matter is that many of the western farmers prefer to sell much of their grain rather than to feed it to hogs and poultry, with the result that we are unable to fulfil our export contracts and to supply our home market. I have always given the hon. member for Melfort credit for trying to be fair. But in making this statement I feel that he is most unfair and most inconsistent. I have checked the record, and I note that during the war -ears the government at Ottawa has paid to the three western provinces almost S200 million in an effort to maintain production in those western provinces.
When those moneys were being paid to western Canada there were no complaints from the hon. member for Melfort or any other members of his group that such payments were economically unsound. But when the benefits are paid to the eastern farmers it would seem that, according to him, they become economically unsound.
There is no group in the house which has so persistently advocated the paying of subsidies as the group to which the hon. member belongs. In fact, this is the first time within my recollection that they have disapproved of the payment of subsidies, and just why they choose to pick on the farmers of the eastern provinces I am at a loss to understand.
The minister has stated that, in order to finish beef cattle already on the farms in eastern Canada, it is necessary for the farmers in the eastern provinces to buy fifty per cent more grain than they have bought in former years. Many of those feeders come from the western provinces. If we cannot buy our grain at reasonable prices, then we cannot continue to raise hogs and poultry and to feed beef cattle.
The hon. member for Melfort knows that, for reasons which need not be mentioned by me, the eastern farmers cannot compete successfully with western farmers in the growing of grain. He also knows that in this very year the farmers in many parts of Quebec and 83166-375
Ontario are facing the possibility of crop failure, owing to a wet season. He knows very well that in this very year there are many parts of Quebec and Ontario, and of the maritime provinces in which there is very little grain sown; and much of .the grain that has been sown was put in the ground so late that it is almost certain to produce a light crop.
If the government were to do what is advocated by the hon. member for Melfort the farmers of eastern Canada would be put out of business so far as the raising of hogs and poultry, and. ithe feeding of beef cattle are concerned. We would not be able to compete in the markets of the world.
The farmers in the eastern provinces, and especially those in Ontario and Quebec, should be most thankful that at this particular time we have not a C.C.F. government at Ottawa. They should feel fortunate indeed that a Liberal government holds office, with a policy which has assisted the farmers and which will continue to assist them, so that they will be able to buy their grain at prices which will permit them to compete in the markets of the world.
I wish to tell the hon. member for Melfort, who is the chief spokesman for the farmers in the C.C.F. that the farmers of Ontario and Quebec will not soon forget the statement he has made with respect to the payment of subsidies to farmers in the eastern provinces.
It was just that it was not economically sound.

I am sure the statement of the hon. member for Melfort will be long remembered by the farmers in the eastern provinces. I trust the minister will give consideration to giving further assistance to the farmers in the east in order that they may be able to continue to raise hogs and poultry, and to feed beef cattle.
I know the government is trying to get away from wartime subsidies. However I would ask the minister, this year if possible, to give consideration to the matter. If he feels that he cannot continue to pay subsidies, I would ask him at least to continue to pay freight rates from the head of the lakes to the eastern provinces. I would ask him what that item amounts to.

speechtext:
In order briefly to advise my hon. friend just where the matter stands perhaps I should place on the record the recommendations which have been made by the engineers of the department. It is a short statement which I think I can get through in two or three minutes, and then I will give my hon. friend the result of the meeting with the delegation.
The reconstruction of transportation facilities leading to and crossing the Strait of Oanso has been under investigation by the engineer, design and capital construction, of the Department of Transport for the past year. This officer has now submitted a complete report covering his investigations.
The strait is approximately fifteen miles long with an average width of some 3.500 feet and with varying depths of from 150 to 200 feet in its narrow sections. Maximum surface velocities at certain tidal phases vary from four to five knots per hour. Both sides of the strait are flanked by high rocky country which rises from 400 to 600 feet above sea level on the west side and somewhat higher on the east. The high land of the latter is located farther back from the shore line than is the case on the west side with the result that much flatter slopes prevail on the east shore than on the west.
Early in the development of this region, a branch of the Intercolonial railway was extended from New Glasgow to Mulgrave. Subsequently, when the railway line was built in Cape Breton, a railway car ferry service was introduced near the mid-point of the strait connecting Mulgrave and Hawkesbury. Two car-ferries, each carrying three tracks on beam widths of 48 to 46 feet respectively, are in operation at this point.
Ten projects of varying types have been embodied in detail in the report of the engineer. Four of these have been reported by him as having no apparent merit and. no further mention will be made of them. Four of the remaining six are similar in type inasmuch as they contemplate reconstruction of and revision to the main line railway on the west side of the strait in order to reduce existing grades with a consequent reduction in railway operating costs. The construction of a new ferry and associated ferry terminals form a part of each of these projects. The remaining two projects reported consist of (a) a bridge crossing the strait with the necessary revisions to highways and to the railway at either end and (b) the construction of a causeway and a lock structure connecting the two shores providing for through
water-borne traffic together with the revisions to the railway and highways as required.
These two latter mentioned projects envisage very considerable difficulties in construction which are reflected .to a great degree in the high estimated cost of these two types of facilities. The estimated cost of the causeway, lock and approaches at present day costs is given as $35,093,800 while that of the bridge and necessary approaches amounts to $54,208,000. The annual operating deficit on the former has been estimated to be $541,920 with that of the latter at $1,631,000.
In order to construct these projects at the estimated costs, as noted, they would have .to be built some four or five miles north of the present ferry terminals thereby isolating the centres of population now located at these terminals from future traffic.
From the point of view of first cost, which is considered to be excessive and also, as a result of the high annual operating deficits of these two projects, the engineer has reported that neither one can be warranted at this time.
Of the remaining four projects considered the engineer has recommended that project No. 7, as embodied in. his report, should be adopted as it provides the lowest estimated annual operating deficit of these four schemes. The total estimated cost of this project is given as $13,300,000 and the annual operating deficit is computed to be $252,900.
Project No. 7 embodies the following main features:-
1.	Grade relocations between LanSberg and Hopewell combined with the elevation of main line track and railway yard at Stel-larton.
2.	The construction of diversions from the main line railway covering five separate sections between the above mentioned .two points and the west side of the strait.
3.	The construction of a new assembly yard and divisional terminal at Porcupine.
4.	The construction of a new ferry similar in size to that constructed in 1927 for the Pere Marquette Railway for use on the St. Clair river.
5.	The construction of a new ferry .terminal about 300 feet south of the existing terminal at Point Tupper.
6.	The construction of a new or revamped ferry .terminal at Mulgrave together with railway yard extensions southerly toward Pirates harbour.
7.	The remodelling of the newer of the existing ferries to suit new terminal conditions in order to provide a standby for the proposed new ferry.

The purpose of this vote is to assist the municipalities in providing temporary shelter to meet emergency requirements. Immediately after the war w7e had a good many government war buildings which could be converted, and they were converted. In the initial stages, the cities largely bore the cost of conversion. Most cities reached the end of their resources fairly quickly. Since then it has been the practice for the government to make the buildings available and to pay half the cost of converting them into apartments. The practice is for the city to administer the emergency shelter and collect the rents to pay for cost of administration, schools and1 city services to people living in the temporary accommodation.

Wartime Housing attempts to get a programme for the current year established by July 1. That has been the practice for the past two or three years. I wish to quote two or
three short statements because I have no desire to detain the committee with a speech. I begin with a statement which the Prime Minister made on June 19, 1947, When he said:
We stand today at the cross-roads of the world. The release of atomic energy marks the opening of a new' life. Whether the new age will be one of unprecedented progress in human welfare or one of unparalleled destruction depends more than all else on whether the affairs of the nations are to be based on a Christian or a pagan philosophy. If we cease to be Christian countries we are doomed.
I believe that the vast majority of Canadians will agree with that statement. There are very few Canadians who would venture to dispute those words.
But, with regard to UNESCO, which means the united nations educational, scientific and cultural organization, I may say that the director general is Julian Huxley and the magazine Time states that he is a scientific atheist. He has made the statement that Darwin made it possible to dispense with the idea of God. For the justification of our moral code we no longer have to have recourse to theological revelation. Freud, in combination with Darwin, suffices. This magazine further states that Julian Huxley, the director
Supply-External Affairs

of UNESCO, has placed on its agenda his proposal to reconcile the philosophies of communism and capitalism and to promote the study of psychoanalysis.
It is not a case of communism versus capitalism, but of Christianity versus paganism.
I should like to quote a few words by Professor Laski, who, I believe, is now a director of UNESCO, in his book, "Faith, Reason and Civilization." At age 63 he states:
Given the fact of victory by the united nations, it seems to me inescapable that the Russian idea will play the same part as the principles of 1789 in reconstituting the outlook of the next age. Unless we claim that the churches will renew their hold on men's allegiance-and there is no serious evidence for the validity of such a claim-the Russian idea seems likely to be the pivotal source from which all values will find the means of renewal.
On page 72 he says:
The Christian faith, in its period of power, overcame this consequence-[DOT]
That is, the consequence of the inequality of fortune.
-by offering to the common man the secret consolation of heaven. But now that the basis upon which that faith was built has crumbled before critical examination, neither the churches nor any other religious organizations can hope to effect the work of renovation.
Those are the views of pagan philosophers. I am not denouncing these men for the views they hold. They have, of course, as much right to their views as I have to mine. I object, however, to the spending of public money to give them the advantage of spreading those pagan ideas among the people of the world.
In contrast, I should like to give two brief quotations. One is by Christopher Dawson, and I take him to be the same Christopher Dawson who, some years ago was editor of the London Times. He said:
By democracy we mean not merely self-government but rather that particular form of government which was based on the ideal of personal liberty. The roots of liberty lie deep in the soil of western Christendom, so that it is impossible to understand it right if we separate it from its religious and cultural background. The whole democratic tradition derived its strength from the Christian belief in the absolute and unique value of the human individual soul which infinitely transcends all wealth and power and glory of the world.
And, finally, the Italian Christian politician Luigi Sturzo wrote, quite recently:
Without the basis of a true Christianity, a true form of Christian democracy could not develop, particularly because modern democracy is the fruit of Christian civilization and has little in common with the pre-Christian classieo-Mediterranean forms of democracy.
Those are the views of Christian philosophers.

I wish to place that on the record for the benefit of the people, for I believe that with these two last statements, together with that of the Prime Minister, the vast majority of Canadians will agree. As the Prime Minister says, if we cease to be Christian nations we are doomed.

I believe in international cooperation and I believe in educational things. I should like to ask the minister if, in his opinion, the contributions under that heading are being used in a sensible and effective way?

That is something which, under the undertaking we made last year, we owe as an international debt. This is required to pay that debt. As to whether Canada has received value for its contribution is a question about which I suppose opinions might differ. So far, tlie achievements of the organization have not been considered. Another meeting is to take place in Mexico in November. Canada will have a delegation at that meeting, but a most modest delegation.
