I have some observations to make which I should like to compress into the space of about two minutes.
In the first place, I wish to say that I think it is deplorable that we are arriving now within a matter of thirty minutes of prorogation without there having been a really serious debate on Canadian trade policy, particularly when great events are occurring in the world today which may have an influential part in shaping the course of this country's future, particularly in the matter of her prosperity, her development and her relations with the world. I hope the minister will take at least enough time to impart to the committee an enunciation in clear terms of the trade policy of the government, and I invite him to do so with particular reference to two matters. The first is the preparatory conference at Geneva which has been in progress for several months looking to the formation of the international trade organization. We have had no report in the house on the progress made there. I can appreciate that there may be difficulties in making an extended report, in view of the negotiations there. But it is a matter of tremendous importance to this country. It would have been well, I think, if parliament had been invited to subscribe to some principles which might have been a guide to the Canadian delegation at Geneva. At the present time it seems to me that the head of the Canadian delegation there must be in some difficulty in proceeding to negotiate with the delegations of other countries, in the absence of some clear indication on the part of parliament as to where it stands with reference to future trade policies.
The other matter to which I wish to refer has to do with the dangers incident to the rather lopsided' trade position in which Canada finds herself at the present time. I do not intend to belabour the point. It was touched on once or twice-altogether too briefly, I think-during the budget debate. I refer to the fact that our relationship with the United States, the country with which we do by far our biggest trade, leaves us in a position in which we have a substantial and growing adverse balance in respect of our commodity trade. That adverse trading balance last year was by far the largest in the history
Supply-Trade and Commerce

of this country, andi it is still growing. The deficit in 1946 jumped to $603,000,000; and in the first four months of this year, 1947, the trading deficit on commodity account only with the United States was $303,000,000. If the present rate continues, the deficit for the entire year 1947 will amount to $900,000,000. That is a serious situation. Different members of the house recentlj' asked the Minister of Finance for some statement as to Canada's position in this regard, but we have not been given any such statement. This matter ds of the utmost importance to Canada, and I hope the minister will take time to give the committee some clear enunciation of government policy in reference to it.

The question regarding the international trade conference at Geneva was asked; of my colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and bis answer appears at page 2000 of Hansard, I can read that answer. The conference at Geneva is being participated in by officials of the Department of External Affairs, the Department of Finance and the Department of Trade and Commerce. At that time my colleague said:
As to whether it will be possible for me to make or table a report on the discussions of the preliminary conference in London, that is something I would have to consider, because, being only one of the members of the conference, we shall have to see to it that we do not publicize anything which it might not be agreeable to the other conferees to have publicized before the line of conduct decided upon at that conference has been implemented in the negotiations at Geneva.
In connection with the matter of trade, Canada's over-all position with all countries practically balances. It is true that there is a very great adverse balance with the United States, and that is something which is giving myself and my colleagues of finance and external affairs, both of whom are closely connected with the matter, very great concern. We cannot stop our people from buying in the United States except by the usual way of imposing tariffs. But we can do our utmost to persuade our people to make their purchases in sterling countries, particularly the United Kingdom, and countries to which we have made loans. We are doing that, and the whole matter is receiving the earnest and serious consideration of the department. We are also pressing in every possible way our sales to hard currency countries such as South Africa. That is a sterling country, of course, but it is backed by gold. Our trade with South Africa has increased very greatly in the past few years, and at the present time

that country is our second largest cash customer. We are also increasing our trade definitely and substantially with all the countries of Latin America.
I do not think I can say much further at the moment. The two main things I want to emphasize are that we are trying to buy as much as possible from the United Kingdom and the countries to which we have made loans, and to make as many sales as possible to hard currency countries.

If the department is seeking to expand our imports from the United Kingdom the figures do not indicate that it is meeting with very much success this year. Our imports from 'the United Kingdom in the first four months of 1946-I am speaking of commodities-amounted to S68,000,000. In the first four months of 1947 they had fallen to $51,000,000, or a drop of about one-quarter in our total commodity imports from the United Kingdom in the first four months of this year as compared with the first four months of 1946. This does not indicate that the department is experiencing much success in trying to redress our present lopsided trade position. We are continuing to increase our imports from the United States, boosting our adverse trade position with that country, and at the same time our purchases of commodities in the United Kingdom show a substantial decrease.
May I now return to the first point on which I asked the minister for a statement. All he has given us is a reiteration of a statement made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs a matter of about three months ago, in which that right hon. gentleman said, in effect, that he did not feel free to make any statement to the house concerning the preliminary conference at London which preceded the conference at Geneva of the nations meeting there with a view to laying the foundations of an international trade organization. We were not told anything about the outcome of the London preparatory conference. We have not as yet been told anything with regard to the progress of the Geneva conference. The point I am making is this, and to me it is a matter of the utmost importance, not only for today, but for the years ahead. Parliament has not been given any report on the instructions that were given to the Canadian delegates to Geneva. Parliament has not been asked to give them any guidance. Parliament has not 'been given any statement on government policy. Parliament has not been asked to give approval or disapproval to any instructions given those delegates. This matter is

Supply-Trade and Commerce
far too important for Canada and the world to be ignored in that way. Even at this late hour I say it is most deplorable that there has not been a proper debate on this subject and a proper enunciation of government policy.

I wish to ask the minister one question before the item is carried. It has to do with one feature of the British wheat agreement. I am speaking now from memory, but I understand that the price is fixed at SI .55 a bushel for the years 1945, 1946 and 1947, but that for the year 1948 it is fixed only as regards the minimum; that is, that it will not be less than SI .25. I understand it is required in the agreement that there be a meeting and a decision by December of this year with respect to the price for the 1948 crop.
I should like the minister to outline to the committee, if he will, the attitude of the government with respect to the price that will be fixed for the 1948 crop. The fact is that for three years the western wheat farmer has been receiving, under the British wheat agreement much less, about a dollar per bushel less than the world price. The government is now going to enter into discussions with the British government in December with respect to the price of wheat for next year. I would like the minister to tell us what he can as to the attitude of the government toward the settlement of that price. It is indicated in the agreement that the British government are to have regard to the conditions obtaining in previous years. I presume this means that they would have regard to the excess of the world price over the price Britain has paid. In view of the fact that the 1948 price will have to be settled; in view of the fact that we have been required to accept a price very much less than the world price, I ask the minister to tell us the attitude of the department and the government as to price in approaching that question next December.

I think the leader of the opposition, in asking his question, has answered it. The attitude of the government is that we are relying on the "having regard to" clause in the contract, so that, in our negotiations for settlement of the 1948 price some time before the end of this year the fact that wheat grown by the western farmer has been sold at a price less than the world price will be taken into consideration when the 1948 price is arrived at. These discussions will, I believe, be entered into late this summer or in the early fall.

Can the minister say now that the price will be higher than the price at which the government has sold the crops of
1945, 1946 and 1947, in view of the fact that we have been taking a lower price? I expect the government will try to get a higher price for the 1948 crop. Can the minister say that?

We have gone through only one year now of the two years at the SI.55 price. There is still another year to be taken into consideration. However I know .that those who will be carrying on these negotiations for the govenment will endeavour to get as fair a return for the Canadian producer as can be obtained, always having regard to the price at which wheat was sold in the first two years of the contract.
Can the minister say what the world price is today?
Yesterday it was $2.63 a bushel.
Can the minister say whether he will undertake to get as much as the world price now is for the 1948 crop?

I cannot say what will be achieved or what will be undertaken; but I may say that the British minister of food, speaking in the house at Westminster, said on July 1:
I feel confident that at the end of the four years both we and the Canadian farmers will find the prices negotiated and to be negotiated under that contract will have turned out to be a just and equitable bargain, immensely beneficial to both parties.

That may be his opinion; but the Canadian people will need some persuasion if they are to be made to think that western farmers have been treated fairly in the matter of wheat prices in this arrangement. Can the minister say, in respect of this 160 million bushels a year that they have been selling at SI.55 per bushel under the British wheat agreement-I presume the world price has averaged more than a dollar more than that-whether in the 1948 price we shall get as much as the average of the world price during the first three years?

I cannot say what we shall get. I know that the negotiations will be carried on to get the best possible deal for the wheat grower. The leader of the opposition mentioned that the average price was approximately $1 a bushel less. I believe it is about seventy-seven cents, on the average, less.
If we have taken seventy-seven cents less than the world price for two or three years can the minister say-

That is only one year.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
Well, whatever period it is. Will the minister try to get at least that much in addition to the present $1.55?

Well, I did not
negotiate this agreement, myself. But I know -at least I think-that my colleague who did negotiate it and who will be carrying on the negotiations will be endeavouring to get what the hon. member is suggesting.
Who negotiated it?

The Minister of
Agriculture.
I should like to speak, Mr. Chairman, but it has nothing to do with wheat.
Let us finish this first, please.
The minister said he had nothing to do with negotiating it.
I did not say I had nothing to do with it.
The minister said he did not negotiate it.
That is correct.
Who did?

The preliminary negotiations were carried on by me and by my colleague the Minister of Agriculture. In the later negotiations, when the final arrangements were arrived at, the Minister of Agriculture carried on those negotiations.
Were the final negotiations and prices arrived at communicated to the minister before they were accepted by the Minister of Agriculture.
Yes, they were.

There are a number of questions I should like to ask the minister in connection with what he has said to the leader of the opposition. He has stated that the average world price during the past year has been approximately seventy-seven cents higher than that paid under the British agreement.
Correct.
How does he arrive at that figure of seventy-seven cents? He has told my leader that the world price today is approximately $2.63. Has it not been higher than that during the past year?
Yes.
What has been the high point in world price during the past year?

When the contract was under negotiation the price was $1.80 to $1.90.

The tables the minister has placed on Hansard do not answer what I have asked, although they do answer a question of which I had given notice. I had' asked as to how much wheat had been sold each week in the past three weeks to countries other than Great Britain.
The minister stated that over a considerable period of time the price was not more than $1.80 on the world market. When was the last occasion within the last year when the world price was as low as $1.80.
I have not the figures in detail, but the crop year last August started a't $2.05.
What was the high?
The high during the year was $3.10.
In United States funds?
No, Canadian funds.
What is it now?
It was $2.58 this afternoon.
I object strenuously to a department such as the Department of Trade and Commerce being brought in at the last moment.
It was not my wish.

I am not going to enter into a controversy, because no one wants to father the fact that this important department has not come in before. When the general discussion took place in regard, to the wheat agreement, representations were made by the leader of the opposition and others on this side that reconsideration should be given to paying the participation certificates on the 1945 crop instead of waiting until 1949 or 1950. When the matter was brought up, the Minister of Agriculture said that, in the light of changing conditions, consideration would be given by the government to making some .provision along that line. Having regard to the condition in which the prairie provinces find themselves as a result of drought this year, is the government giving consideration to paying the 1945 participation certificates this year?
The government has not decided to change its policy, which is embodied in legislation, to include 1945 in the five-year pool.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I move:
That the house do not adjourn at eleven o'clock today.

Motion agreed to.
Supply-Trade and Commerce
The house in committee of supply, Mr. Golding in the chair.

I should like to say a word or two about the matter of export permits which was brought up a day or two ago, particularly iwith regard to registered breeding stock going to the United States. Several shipments -from western Ontario were held up because the shippers had not export permits. An order in council was passed which cleaned up the matter, but one shipper had eighty head of dairy cattle which were held up for two weeks. At the end of that time some of -the cattle were not in condition t-o ship and he had to take a considerable loss. We need United States dollars, and we should not put anything in the way of farmers who are trying to export our goods to the United States.
On the other hand, vegetables and fruits are coming into this country from the United States. Practically every year -the dumping duties on tomatoes, early potatoes and other vegetables are put on too late. In- other words, our Canadian farmer gets the raw end of the deal practically every -time. Representations have been imade this year with regard to certain articles, but action was not taken as early as it should have been. A week and a half ago there were thirty carloads of tomatoes on -the Toronto market and field tomatoes were coming in from the Essex area. I called up the department about the matter, and they said that nothing could be done about- tomatoes because they did not come under the dumping duties regulation. The farmer gets stung either way.
Blueberries are being brought into this country and yet they are grown here. We would save exchange if money was not being spent for United States blueberries, and there are other things that could be -mentioned.
Before the war I and a number of others were interested in the export of honey to England. That is a thing of the past and I doubt if we shall be able to get back into that market. We are going to reach a time when there will be a surplus of honey in Canada. There is a market in the United States at the present time. I am not saying that the export restrictions on honey should be removed, but do not let us get into the fix where we are stuck with honey and have not a market. I believe a few token shipments should be permitted. I know of a man in California who would like to get some of our buckwheat honey, which is not usually used as a table

honey in this country, for medicinal purposes. I took this matter up with the export permit people, but I was refused a permit today because they said there was a shortage in Canada.
The farmers in Middlesex county have a lot of good fat cattle. I attended a farmers' picnic yesterday and they told me that they are worried about the cattle business. They realize that we should retain the British market, but they do not like the idea of the packers -being able to drop the price a cent or two in a week or a day. They believe that if the United States market were opened, say for a week, that would not occur. I would suggest that the first time the price of beef cattle drops the restrictions on shipments to the United States should be lifted for a week to see what happens to the cattle market. I am asking this for the protection of farmers in Ontario.

I should like to say a couple of words with regard to the wheat agreement. I wish to draw attention to the rising costs which are faced by farmers. Our farmers want stabilization more than anything else, and the wheat agreement was the finest thing we have yet got. It is the best break that has ever come to the western farmer, the stabilization of wheat prices and an agreement for five years. We know that SI.35 was never recognized as parity; it was only the price set with participation certificates over a period of five years. Parity to the farmer means a share of the national income, approximately equal to the proportion of the farmers to the national population. The government will have to see that the prices of things the farmer has to buy, his gas, his oil, his binder twine and so forth, are kept at reasonable levels. The prices of these things have gone up. If you are to bind the farmer to the agreement, which the farmer wants-he is quite pleased with the controlled market-you will have to control the other fellow's prices. If you let the other fellow set his own prices it will not be a square deal for the farmers. I do not want to take up a lot of time; I could speak for forty minutes on this. You have given the farmer the British wheat agreement which is the best step that has ever been taken. I have lived on the prairies for pretty nearly thirty years. I know what I am talking about. You have taken the speculation out of grain and the farmer is getting a set price for five years. The farmer is better off today than he has been for some considerable time. The war did that. I deplore the fact that we had to have a war to bring that about. If you want to keep the farmer in a healthy position, then you must

Supply-Trade and Commerce
control the other fellows who are going to make that $1.35 look like nothing.

Will the minister say just a word as to the nature of the industrial development division?

This is a branch which has been established in the department, headed by a particularly able man to keep in close touch with all the industrial development work in the various centres throughout Canada, with the provinces and the railways.
What does it mean "to keep in touch with the various centres"? Is he guiding or stimulating or what?

Does this mean that what we charge for the use of these elevators is $700,000 short of what it costs us? I see that there is some equipment in the item. How much do we lose in operating these, and why do we need' to lose anything? Why not charge enough to cover the cost?

Canadian government travel bureau-
JiOl. To assist in promoting the tourist business in Canada, $650,000.

I wish to ask the minister if it is a matter of policy to maintain close contact between the Canadian government travel bureau and other departments of government whose functions have a bearing on the attraction of tourists to Canada. I think we have at the head of the Canadian government travel bureau a very competent director in Mr. Dolan. Every one of us admits the importance of this tourist traffic to Canada. It is one of the biggest industries we have and it has a great future ahead of it. I am thinking more of keeping in closest contact with government departments which are in a position to assist the work of the bureau in stimulating tourist traffic coming to this country. I may give an illustration. Last September I was in Nanaimo. Nanaimo formerly used to receive a generous share of the United States tourist trade; but latterly, because of neglect of the harbour, the businessmen of that city, speaking through the board of trade, were complaining strongly that they were losing part of the United States tourist traffic they had previously enjoyed. In a situation of that kind, is some attempt made to keep these government departments in contact with one another, so that these departments whose functions have a bearing on the attraction of tourists to Canada are doing their utmost to assist the work of Mr. Dolan and the staff of the Canadian travel bureau?

The bureau does keep in close touch with other branches of government, such as national parks; and along the same line, we keep in very close touch with the operations of the provincial bureaux. Last fall we originated the idea of having a joint conference of provincial tourist organizations with us in Ottawa. It was very successful, and there has been a desire from all provinces to repeat it this year. We propose to call another conference in October.

That is all to the good.
The matter of cooperation between the dominion bureau and the provincial departments is commendable, but I do not think the minister has my point. I am thinking about other federal departments. The responsibility for keeping harbours in proper condition belongs to the public wojks department. Is some attempt being made by these depart-

ments to keep in touch with the travel bureau and to accept suggestions which will enable the bureau to carry on the function of attracting more tourists?

I am told that such
an attempt is being made.

Customs and excise divisions-
244. General administration, $1,168,648.

There are two inquiries
I wish to make on specific matters. They affect the administration of the Department of National Revenue in Toronto. One has to do with income tax and the other with customs. I will deal with income tax first. This has to do with salaries of staff.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCANN (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Customs and excise first.

My inquiry has to do
with existing bonded warehouse facilities in Toronto. At the present time, I am informed, the bonded warehouse facilities there are quite inadequate. The business which the present facilities have been called upon to provide for has been growing very rapidly. In fact, I am told that in recent years it has practically doubled. In 1942 there were 800 entries a day and fourteen checkers. Today, I am informed, the number of daily entries is 1,500 and the number of checkers has not increased. In other words, the same staff is called upon to handle practically double the work. That is on the aspect of staff.
In addition, there is the question of accommodation. At the (present time there is a
C.N.R. bonded warehouse at Simcoe and Wellington, C.P.R. accommodation in the dominion public building on Front Street, and a C.N. express office in the same building. According to my information, the accommodation is quite inadequate and, by reason of the insufficiency of both accommodation and staff, there is a good deal of complaint about the slowness of the service. Sometimes, I understand, there are delays of three days to a week in obtaining delivery of goods after they have been cleared through the customs. That is a serious matter for a good many importers, and I would urge upon the minister that steps be taken to increase the staff and improve the accommodation.
We must bear in mind that this is a service which provides the country with revenue, and those who are paying the revenue through customs duties have a right to expect that

Supply-National Revenue
facilities shall be provided and that the bonded warehouses will give good and efficient service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: The points that have been brought to my attention by the hon. member, we are quite aware of. The trouble has been due, in the main to the difficulty of securing facilities to meet the increased amount of business offering. That applies both to the tax division and to customs and excise. I cannot say that we have had any particular complaints as to delay or shortage of staff, but we will inquire into the matter.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: I believe the question was dealt with fairly well in the answer I gave. During the war years, cigarettes seized were turned over to the Red Cross for distribution. The experience of the department following the first great war in handing cigarettes over to other institutions did not work out very well, because the people for w'hom they were intended never got them, and the very fact that Canadian manufacturers pay an excise tax is another reason why we have not been distributing them. I will look further into the matter.

It is my desire to voice a grievance with respect to the Department of National Revenue. The minister is familiar with the case I have to present at this time. Some months ago, in the city of Regina a war veteran, an air force officer who had been shot down over Germany and had spent twenty months in a prisoners of war camp, received a reestablishment credit or the blessing of the department to reestablish himself as a customs broker in that city. The business in Regina is quite ample to look after this young man's business if he had been able to receive a licence from the licensing advisory committee established for that purpose by the Department of National Revenue. There are only two customs brokers in that city and one operates exclusively for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company. The licensing advisory committee refused this young man's application for a licence to become a customs broker in my city, even though he was eminently qualified for that work. The reason given by the licensing advisory committee was that the father of the young air force officer was an employee of the customs branch at the city of Regina. That, of course, is correct.
The point I wish to make is this. By virtue of what the licensing advisory committee decided, in accordance with the regulations of the Department of National Revenue, they continued a monopoly in a very lucrative business in the city of Regina which could be advantageously used for the reestablishment of this young man. I do not intend to introduce a debate. I just intend to offer in a few minutes, a few words of wisdom to the government. I believe they can use some occasionally. The first one is in connection with the question of bringing in some of the war assets from the United States. The United States War Assets Corporation made available to the public some of their 16-ply nylon tires from the big aeroplanes. These were discovered to be most useful as tractor tires, and some of our smaller business men in the west undertook to bring them over. 1 do not know whether or not there are any left, but if there are I believe it would be advisable for the government to consider bringing those in duty free for that purpose. A good deal of duty has been paid on those which have already come in.
The other matter I wish to speak about is the question of duty on egg crate fillers made from pulp. A great deal of our pulp is shipped to the United States, and I understand that a higher rate is paid for it than is paid by Canadian manufacturers. I am not sure of that, but it is what I have been told. Yet when their fillers come in, they are dutiable. It would appear that Canadian raw materials going over there for processing and then

coming back here as an end product should be available to the Canadian people without duty. I hope the minister will consider that.

speechtext:
As the hon. gentleman no doubt realizes, there has been a reclassification with reference to the Montreal office. I find now that of the occupants of the twenty-two key positions in the Montreal office, eleven are French. They are:	Messrs. Another one is of half English and half French descent. That is Mr. Pope. I am informed by the director general of the Montreal office- and 'he has been in the office for something over thirty years, I believe-that there have never before been as many French-Canadians in key positions as there are today, and that the reorganization we have made has already increased that representation. I appreciate the difficulties there are in that particular office in Montreal, the largest office we have in Canada. We do a bigger business there in the year than the Canadian Pacific does in the whole of Canada. It is important that efficiency must be the first consideration in regard to the personnel of that office. 1 recognize, too, that the efficiency will be improved if a holder of an office there is bilingual, whether he is descended from either French or English forebears. We are attempting in. the reorganization plan to give a fair proportion to both French and English. But we must always keep in mind that efficiency is the first test. I think the men who have approached me on this particular subject will agree with me that it is difficult to get the type of people we want who are bilingual. I should like to bring to the attention of the minister a situation involving the salaries which are paid to accountants in the income tax office at Toronto. I am informed that recently a number of accountants were brought in who had been formerly on the staff of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply. Their salaries in that department were $2,700 per annum, and when they were brought on the staff of the income tax office at Toronto they came in at the same salary. But they were placed under supervisors who proceeded to instruct them in their new duties, and the supervisors receive a salary of only $2,100 a year. I am told that situation is continuing. The supervising officials of the income tax office are receiving salaries of $2,100. These accountants brought in to work under their supervision are being paid $2,700. That is a 83166-376i
most anomalous situation, and I submit that some corrective measures must be applied promptly. My information goes farther and indicates that there is a great deal of disaffection and unrest over this situation on the part of the members of the staff who were there before, particularly those engaged in supervisory capacities.

I wish to say a word on this, just following what my colleague the hon. member for Eglinton has said. First, let me say I believe in the film board. I think it performs a duty which the commercial people do not perform; but I am not at all convinced that the film board needs to do its own production. speechtext: The policy of t'he film board is both production and distribution, and, of course, administration. In some instances, in the matter of production competitive prices are asked from the private agencies, and I may say that, from a comparison of the costs, the film board can produce as cheaply as any agency in Canada. There has been a good deal in the newspapers lately to the effect that the film board should go out of the production field and be entirely a distributing agency. I cannot say I agree with that view, because our costs compare favourably with those of other agencies. We have passed a lot of estimates and have looked upon the mercenary side of life. During the last two or three weeks we have been sitting long and arduous hours, and I should like to say a word on behalf of the page boys. These boys have had experience in parliamentary life, but many of them have been deprived of their schooling. After which the Honourable the Deputy Governor General was pleased, to close the third session of the twentieth [parliament of the Dominion of Canada with the following speech:
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
The restoration of peace and world recovery have not proceeded as speedily as had been hoped for. Failure to conclude peace settlements with Germany and Austria has complicated the political and economic situation, not only in Europe, but throughout the world. Several countries, including Canada, have approved treaties of peace with Italy, Rou-mania. Hungary and Finland.
In Europe, the delay in the re-establishment of industries has continued to affect adversely the balance of foreign trade and of international payments. The severe winter and the shortage of necessities, particularly of food, have added to human suffering, and aggravated the problems of relief and rehabilitation.
Unsettled world conditions have been reflected' in many of the measures you have been called' upon to consider at the session now being: concluded.
On June 30, the united nations relief and rehabilitation administration came to an end.. The need for relief, however, has not ended. In recognition of this need, parliament has made a substantial appropriation for the purchase of food and other essentials of life required by peoples of war-devastated lands. Parliament has also approved Canadian membership in the international refugee organization.
Canada is participating fully in the activities of the economic and social council, the atomic energy commission, and other agencies of the united nations. Our country is also effectively represented at the international conference on trade and employment at Geneva.
As a result of the deliberations of a special session of the general assembly of the united nations, a committee, on which Canada is represented, was created to prepare a report on Palestine.
An important feature of the session has been the removal, in an orderly manner, of the majority of controls and restrictions in force during and immediately after the war. To guard against sudden and excessive increases in the cost of living, and for other reasons, certain emergency orders and regulations have been continued for a further transitional period.
Another important development has been the action taken to encourage immigration. The Government's^ policy involves the careful selection of immigrants and adjustment of their numbers to the absorptive capacity of the country. Practical steps have also been taken to relieve the lot of many displaced persons and refugees.
Notwithstanding the unsettled conditions abroad, employment and national income at home have remained at high levels. The demand for the products of our primary industries has, in almost all oases, been sustained. Towards stabilizing the incomes of those engaged in agriculture, measures relating to the Canadian wheat board, and to the sale and export of certain other agricultural products have been enacted. The Fisheries Prices Support Act is being brought into operation. The maintenance of our prosperity will increasingly depend upon how conditions develop in other parts of the world.
In the past few months, in most industries, Canada has fortunately enjoyed a relatively wide measure of industrial peace. Preliminary consideration has been given in parliament to an important measure to provide more effective machinery for the settlement of industrial disputes and the adjustment of differences between employers and employees. A similar measure will be introduced at the next session.
The Government has continued to give constant attention to meeting the need for housing. To this end, substantial amendments have been: made to the National Housing Act.
A further measure of social security has been provided by important amendments to the Old' Age Pensions Act. Increases have been made in-
Governor General's Speech.

the amount of pension, and also in the amount of other income permitted to pensioners. In addition, the pensionable age for blind persons has been lowered from forty to twenty-one years.
The Civil Service Superannuation Act has been amended to include additional categories of public servants, and to permit retirement at an earlier age than heretofore. Comprehensive changes have also been made to increase the security provided by the Act. Statutory provision has been made for the veteran's preference in appointments to the civil service, and to permit of annual increases in remuneration to temporary employees.
Steady progress 'has been made in placing the defence forces on a peace-time basis. The Department of National Defence Act has been amended to provide for the consolidation of the administration of the department, and for the establishment of a defence research board.
During the session, an important announcement of joint Canada-United States policy respecting cooperation in defence was made at Washington by the president and at Ottawa by the prime minister.
Other important measures enacted during the session include bills concerning a dominion coal board, a maritime commission, the Canadian broadcasting corporation, conservation of natural resources, loan adjustments with certain of the provinces, the Patent Act, Penitentiaries and the Criminal Code. A benevolent fund from army canteen and other service funds has been established.
The representation of the people in the House of Commons has been readjusted on a basis which will more effectively maintain the historic principle of representation by population.
The question of human rights and fundamental freedoms, and the manner in which those * obligations, accepted by all members of the united nations, may best be implemented, has been given preliminary consideration by a . special joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons. It is the intention of my ministers to recommend the reappointment of this committee at the next session of parliament.
Members of the House of Commons:
I thank you for the provision you have made for all essential services.
A most gratifying achievement of the session now concluding has been the substantial reduction in the level of taxation on personal incomes, which became effective on the first of July, and which was made possible by the drastic reduction of public expenditures. At the end of the year, the tax on excess profits will be removed.
Authority to conclude tax agreements with the provinces has been vested in the government. Seven of the nine provinces have signified their intention to conclude such agreements.
A bill to revise the income tax law was introduced in order to permit of study and consideration of its provisions between now and the next session.
Honourable Members of the Senate:
Members of the House of Commons:
The recent visit of the president of the United States to Ottawa was deeply appreciated by the citizens of Canada. The visit afforded renewed evidence of the close and cordial relations of our two countries.
My ministers have been pleased to welcome a delegation from the national convention of Newfoundland. Members of the delegation are exploring the possibility of finding a basis, which would be mutually acceptable, for the federal union of Newfoundland with Canada.
The people of Canada have learned with great pleasure of the betrothal of Her Royal Highness The Princess Elizabeth to Lieutenant Philip Mountbatten. As Her Royal Highness and Lieutenant Mountbatten continue to face the future with its duties and responsibilities, it will be the wish of all that health, happiness, and divine guidance may gladden their path through life.
Amid the uncertainties and perils of these troubled times, I pray that the guidance of Almighty God may be vouchsafed to our country and all the nations.
This concluded the third session of the twentieth parliament.
AWARDS GRANTED TO PERSONNEL OF THE CANADIAN ARMED FORCES From 10th September, 1939 to 31st March, 1947

HIS MAJESTY THE KING has been pleased to award the Victoria Cross (Posthumous) to Lieutenant Robert Hampton Gray, R.CN.V.R. "for great bravery in leading an attack to within 50 feet of a Japanese destroyer in the face of intense anti-aircraft fire, thereby sinking the destroyer although he was hit and his aircraft [DOT]on fire and, finally, himself killed. He was one of the gallant company of naval airmen who, from December, 1944, fought and beat the Japanese from Palembang to Tokyo.
The actual incident took place in the Onagawa Wan on 9th August, 1945. Gray was leader of the attack which he pressed home in the face of fire from shore batteries and at least 8 warships. With his aircraft in flames, he nevertheless obtained at least one direct hit which sank his objective."

The KING has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the VICTORIA CROSS to:
Honorary Captain John Weir Foote, Canadian Chaplain Services.
Honorary Captain Foote, Canadian Chaplain Services, was regimental chaplain with The Royal Hamilton Light Infantry at Dieppe on 19th August, 1942.
Upon landing on the beach under heavy fire, he attached himself to the regimental aid post wihich had been set up in a slight depression on the beach, but which was only sufficient to give cover to men lying down. During the subsequent period of approximately eight hours, while action continued, this officer not only assisted the regimental medical officer in ministering to the wounded in the regimental aid

post, but time and again left this shelter to inject morphine, give first aid and carry wounded personnel from the open beach to the regimental aid post. On these occasions, with utter disregard for his personal safety, Honorary Captain Foote exposed himself to an inferno of fire and saved many lives by his gallant efforts.
During the action, as the tide went out, the regimental aid post was moved to the shelter of a stranded landing craft. Honorary Captain Foote continued tirelessly and courageously to carry wounded men from the exposed beach to the cover of the landing craft. Also he removed wounded from inside the landing craft when ammunition had been set on fire by enemy shells. When landing craft appeared, he carried wounded from the regimental aid post to the landing craft through heavy fire with no consideration for his own safety.
On several occasions this officer had the opportunity to embark but returned to the beach as his chief concern was the care and evacuation of the wounded. He refused a final opportunity to leave the shore, choosing to suffer the fade of the men he had ministered to for over three years.
Honorary Captain Foote personally saved many lives by his efforts and his example inspired all around him. Those who observed him state that the calmness of this heroic man as he walked about, collecting the wounded on the fire swept beach will never be forgotten.
The KING has been graciously pleased to approve the award of the VICTORIA CROSS (posthumously) to:
H.6008 Warrant Officer Class II (Company
Sergeant-Major) John Robert Osborn.
1 Battalion, The Winnipeg Grenadiers.
At Hong Kong on the morning of 19th December, 1941, a Company of the Winnipeg Grenadiers to Which Company Sergeant-Major Osborn belonged became divided during an attack on Mount Butler, a hill rising steeply above sea level. A part of the Company led by Company Sergeant-Major Osborn captured the hill at the point of the bayonet and held it for three hours *when, owing to the superior number of the enemy and to fire from an unprotected flank, the position became untenable. Company Sergeant-Major Osborn and a small group covered the withdrawal and when their turn came to fall back, Osborn single-handed engaged the enemy while the remainder successfully rejoined the Company. Company Sergeant-Major Osborn had to run the gauntlet of heavy rifle and machine gun fire. With no consideration for his own safety he assisted and directed stragglers to the new Company position exposing himself to heavy enemy fire to cover their retirement. Wherever danger threatened he was there to encourage his men.
During the afternoon the Company was cut off from the Battalion and completely surrounded by the enemy who were able to approach to within grenade throwing distance of the slight depression which the Company were holding. Several enemy grenades were thrown which Company Sergeant-Major Osborn picked up and threw back. The enemy threw a grenade which landed in a position where it was impossible to pick it up and return it in time. Shouting a warning to his comrades this gallant Warrant Officer threw himself on the grenade which exploded killing him instantly. His self sacrifice undoubtedly saved the lives [DOT]of many others.
Company Sergeant-Major Osborn was an inspiring example to all throughout the defence which he assisted so magnificently in maintaining against an overwhelming enemy force for over eight and a half hours and in his death he displayed the highest quality of heroism and self-sacrifice.
The KING has been graciously pleased to confer the following award in recognition of most conspicuous bravery:

Pilot Officer Andrew Charles Mynarski (J87544) (deceased).
Home Address: 846 Manitoba Ave., Winnipeg, Man.
"Pilot Officer Mynarski was the mid-upper gunner of a Lancaster aircraft, detailed to attack a target at Cambrai in France, on the night of 12th June, 1944. The aircraft was attacked from below and astern by an enemy fighter and ultimately came down in flames.
As an immediate result of the attack, both port engines failed. Fire broke out betweem the mid-upper turret and the rear turret, as well as in the port wing. The flames soon became fierce and the captain ordered the crew to abandon the aircraft.
Pilot Officer Mynarski left his turret and went towards the escape hatch. He then saw that the rear gunner was still in his turret and apparently unable to leave it. The turret was, in fact, immovable, since the hydraulic gear had been put out of action when the port engines failed, and the manual gear had been broken by the gunner in his attempts to escape.
Without hesitation, Pilot Officer Mynarski made his way through the flames in an endeavour to reach the rear turret and release the gunner. Whilst so doing, his parachute and his clothing, up to the waist, were set on fire. All his efforts to move the turret and free the gunner were in vain. Eventually the rear gunner clearly indicated to him that there was nothing more he could do and that he should try to save his own life. Pilot Officer Mynarski reluctantly went back through the flames to the escape hatch. There, as a last gesture to the trapped gunner, he turned towards him, stood to attention in his flaming clothing and saluted, before he jumped out of the aircraft. Pilot Officer Mynarski's descent was seen by French people on the ground. Both his parachute and his clothing were on fire. He was found eventually by the French, but was so severely burnt that he died from his injuries.
The rear gunner had a miraculous escape when the aircraft crashed. He subsequently testified that, had Pilot Officer Mynarski not attempted to save his comrade's life, he could have left the aircraft in safety and would, doubtless, have escaped death.
Pilot Officer Mynarski must have been fully aware that in trying to free the rear gunner he was almost certain to lose his own life. Despite this, with outstanding courage and complete disregard for his own safety, he went to the rescue. Willingly accepting the danger, Pilot Officer Mynarski lost his life by a most conspicuous act of heroism which called for valour of the highest order."
